text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

WHY GOOD HANDOFF MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECT SCREENS
WHY GOOD HANDOFF MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECT SCREENS

Handoff is a shared understanding of the product decision. Exporting a polished screen is one part of it, not the point at which responsibility disappears.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Separate a delivered file from an agreed decision
Give ambiguity a place and an owner
Review a real example instead of a generic checklist
Keep a small decision record
Close the loop in the built product
SEPARATE A DELIVERED FILE FROM AN AGREED DECISION

A file can be complete while the team still disagrees about what a button does. That is why I treat handoff as a review of intent, constraints and unresolved behavior. The useful question is whether another person can continue the work without guessing.

Three kinds of uncertainty tend to get mixed together: a design choice that has not been made, a business rule that belongs to someone else, and a technical constraint that has not been checked. Calling all three a design annotation hides who needs to act.

GIVE AMBIGUITY A PLACE AND AN OWNER
Give ambiguity a place and an owner
Question	Decision needed	Likely participant
May a draft omit a required field?	Draft and submission rules	Product and engineering
What happens after access is revoked?	Authorization and recovery behavior	Engineering and product
Which action is primary on mobile?	Task hierarchy	Design with implementation review
What counts as accepted?	Observable release conditions	Design, engineering and QA
REVIEW A REAL EXAMPLE INSTEAD OF A GENERIC CHECKLIST

The Orkest create-lead form is a useful review object because it exposes specific dependencies: an owner, an initial state and a score calculated after saving. The handoff conversation should resolve those behaviors, including what remains after failure. It should not stop at whether the fields match the artboard.

Orkest create-lead screen with grouped contact and qualification fields and a next-step explanation. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

KEEP A SMALL DECISION RECORD

For each consequential change, record the decision, its reason, the affected frame or component and the implementation status. A sentence can be enough. For example: preserve entered values after a recoverable save failure so retrying does not require rebuilding the form.

Do not bury a changed requirement in a chat thread while leaving the old design marked ready. Update the artifact people will actually use, then identify which existing screens or tests need to change.

CLOSE THE LOOP IN THE BUILT PRODUCT

Review the implementation with realistic content, a keyboard and at least one interrupted task. Compare the behavior with the agreed contract, not only the screenshot. Distinguish a visual difference that preserves intent from a behavioral difference that changes the task.

A handoff is useful when it reduces uncertainty and supports continuation. I would evaluate it by the quality of the questions resolved and the decisions retained through implementation, rather than the number of exported screens or pages of annotations.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

WHAT I LEARNED DESIGNING MY PORTFOLIO LIKE A PRODUCT
WHAT I LEARNED DESIGNING MY PORTFOLIO LIKE A PRODUCT

I want a portfolio to help someone evaluate my judgment, not only recognize a visual style. That means treating evidence, navigation and performance as part of the same product.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Give the visitor a question to answer
Keep the visual identity, reduce the evaluation cost
Make the evidence boundary visible
Treat performance as part of access
Choose an honest next improvement
GIVE THE VISITOR A QUESTION TO ANSWER

A recruiter may be asking whether I can handle a particular kind of complexity. A potential client may be checking whether my contribution matches their problem. Those are evaluation tasks. The portfolio should help people find relevant work and understand what it actually demonstrates.

That is why a case study needs a precise scope and an inspectable artifact. A broad statement about strategy is weaker than a concrete decision connected to a form, a record model or a responsive content problem.

KEEP THE VISUAL IDENTITY, REDUCE THE EVALUATION COST

This site uses an editor-inspired workspace with expressive type and motion. I want that personality to remain, while the project and article pages use the same navigation, fonts and interaction language. A strong homepage followed by unrelated inner-page styling makes the experience harder to trust and maintain.

Shared presentation does not mean shared prose. A logistics journey, a consulting website and a Sass utility need different explanations and different kinds of proof.

MAKE THE EVIDENCE BOUNDARY VISIBLE

In the current editorial revision, Figma exports are separated from public derivatives. Screens are selected for the decision they help explain, complete source frames are retained with their dummy content and the source is recorded. Drafts and legacy prototypes are not silently presented as current releases.

Where a matching file is missing, the case keeps the gap visible. Code or an existing website artifact may be better evidence than a design screenshot. No visual placeholder can establish a result that was never measured.

TREAT PERFORMANCE AS PART OF ACCESS

An elaborate interface still needs to be readable and usable on a narrow screen and a slower connection. I use repeatable builds, route checks and browser audits to inspect the implementation. A laboratory score is a measurement of a tested configuration, not a guarantee of everyone's experience.

The current review also separates code readiness from production deployment and Google indexing. Those are different states. A successful local test cannot establish that a search engine has processed a change.

CHOOSE AN HONEST NEXT IMPROVEMENT

The portfolio is still a product with constraints. A screenshot archive can be incomplete, a client example can require permission and a manual accessibility review can remain outstanding. Recording those limits gives the next improvement a clear starting point.

My practical test is whether someone can find a relevant case, explain my contribution, inspect the evidence and decide whether to contact me. The visual identity should support that evaluation rather than become a separate task to solve.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

DESIGNING SERVICE WEBSITES THAT EXPLAIN THE BUSINESS CLEARLY
DESIGNING SERVICE WEBSITES THAT EXPLAIN THE BUSINESS CLEARLY

A service page needs to help someone recognize their situation, understand the scope and decide whether a conversation is worthwhile. A list of capabilities is only the starting material.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Begin with the client's question
Use scope and sequence as evidence
Give the page a useful sequence
Keep proof specific and permission-aware
Carry context into the inquiry
BEGIN WITH THE CLIENT'S QUESTION

A client may arrive with a problem rather than the name of a discipline. Organize the opening around that recognizable situation, then explain what the service includes. Avoid making the visitor translate internal terminology before they can establish fit.

A useful opening also has boundaries. Say what kind of work the service covers and what it does not. Broad claims about solving every business problem make evaluation harder, even when they sound confident.

USE SCOPE AND SEQUENCE AS EVIDENCE

The Morajaa market-entry design includes a named process after its service explanation. The reviewed crop shows how stage titles create a scan while supporting text supplies depth. It is evidence of content hierarchy; it does not independently verify the consultancy's regulatory statements or delivery results.

Morajaa full market-entry service page connects the opening promise, services, process and contact. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

GIVE THE PAGE A USEFUL SEQUENCE
Give the page a useful sequence
Section	Question it should answer
Situation	Is this relevant to my problem?
Scope	What work is actually included?
Approach	What would working together involve?
Proof	What can I inspect to evaluate the claim?
Boundary	What should I not assume?
Next step	What will happen if I make contact?
KEEP PROOF SPECIFIC AND PERMISSION-AWARE

Use a project example because it helps evaluate the service, not because the page has an empty image slot. Explain the contribution and distinguish a design artifact from a commercial result. A screenshot can show a decision without proving a client outcome.

If the strongest material is private, narrow the public account rather than replacing it with an invented result. A clear contribution statement is more useful than a confident but unsupported success story.

CARRY CONTEXT INTO THE INQUIRY

A contact action should follow enough explanation for the person to know what they are asking about. Keep the form proportional to that first conversation. If it preserves a selected service, make that context visible and editable.

Review the mobile reading order and the route back to supporting information. The website should let a careful visitor evaluate the offer without forcing immediate contact or burying the action after repetitive content.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

DESIGNING WEB3 PRODUCTS WITHOUT MAKING USERS FEEL LOST
DESIGNING WEB3 PRODUCTS WITHOUT MAKING USERS FEEL LOST

Start with what the person is trying to do. Explain the wallet or network when it changes the decision, instead of making protocol vocabulary the entrance requirement.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Separate the product task from the mechanism
Keep familiar context around the unfamiliar step
Avoid three kinds of false reassurance
Use product language with inspectable detail
Review the handoff between systems
SEPARATE THE PRODUCT TASK FROM THE MECHANISM

A person may want to join, send, collect or review. A wallet request is a mechanism within that task. Explain why it is needed and what it enables before asking the person to follow it.

This does not mean hiding technical detail. It means placing that detail where it helps a decision. Someone evaluating an address, network or transaction needs access to the relevant specifics; someone establishing basic product fit should not have to decode them first.

KEEP FAMILIAR CONTEXT AROUND THE UNFAMILIAR STEP

Yarsha puts wallet-related activity inside a messaging context. The reviewed token-selection frame identifies assets using names and symbols and offers a search. It gives a concrete discussion point: establish what the person is acting on before any later authorization step.

The complete source frame is included in the Yarsha case. Its balance-like values are dummy content; the useful design question is how a person distinguishes assets before a consequential action.

AVOID THREE KINDS OF FALSE REASSURANCE
Do not imply that connecting a wallet authorizes every later action.
Do not describe an attempted request as a confirmed result.
Do not promise immediate recovery when a wallet, network or external service controls the next transition.
USE PRODUCT LANGUAGE WITH INSPECTABLE DETAIL

Before a consequential action, state what will change and keep relevant destination, asset and amount information available. Afterward, distinguish the known result from an unresolved state. A generic success animation cannot substitute for that explanation.

Technical details should support inspection without becoming the only explanation. Work with engineering to define the actual states and evidence available to the interface. The design should not invent certainty that the integration cannot provide.

REVIEW THE HANDOFF BETWEEN SYSTEMS

Walk through leaving the product for a wallet, rejecting the request, returning after a delay and reopening the original context. Decide which information persists and which actions remain available. Use real integration tests before describing the behavior as complete.

For portfolio writing, keep the same boundary. A source frame can support a claim about visible hierarchy. It cannot independently prove transaction reliability, security or user comprehension. Narrow, inspectable evidence makes a stronger story than an exaggerated Web3 outcome.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

SAAS DASHBOARD EMPTY STATE UX GUIDE
SAAS DASHBOARD EMPTY STATE UX GUIDE

Before writing an empty-state headline, identify what the interface actually knows. The next action should follow the cause, not a reusable illustration.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Write the cause before the call to action
Use a small cause-to-copy worksheet
Inspect a real zero-result frame
Keep the message proportionate
Review the words in a transition
WRITE THE CAUSE BEFORE THE CALL TO ACTION

No data is a description of the display, not an explanation. A new workspace, an over-restrictive filter and a failed request may all leave an empty panel, but they require different messages. Start by writing one sentence about why this result is empty, using only information the application can establish.

Then choose an action that changes that cause. Create your first lead fits an eligible new workspace. Clear filters fits a filtered result. Retry fits some request failures. Using one button for all three can send the person in the wrong direction.

USE A SMALL CAUSE-TO-COPY WORKSHEET
Use a small cause-to-copy worksheet
Known cause	Possible explanation	Relevant action
No matching records	No leads match these filters	Change or clear conditions
No records created	This workspace has no leads yet	Create or import, if permitted
Request failed	We could not load the leads	Retry with retained context
Access is insufficient	Use an approved access explanation	Request access when supported
Setup is incomplete	Name the missing setup step	Continue setup
INSPECT A REAL ZERO-RESULT FRAME

The Yarsha contact-search design reports No contact found while retaining the search context and keyboard. It is a mobile example of the same writing problem, not a SaaS dashboard screenshot. Contacts and Invite are visible, but the frame does not explain whether invitation is the right recovery for this query.

A useful revision discussion would ask whether the person can broaden the search, clear it or understand the Invite route. The image supports those questions; it does not establish that they have already been answered.

Yarsha contact search preserves the entered query, Contacts and Invite tabs, empty result and keyboard. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

KEEP THE MESSAGE PROPORTIONATE

A routine search with no matches rarely needs a large celebratory illustration or a paragraph about the product's value. Name the result, keep the query visible and provide a concise continuation. A first-use state may need more explanation because the person has not yet learned the model.

Avoid blame. Invalid input can be described precisely without suggesting carelessness. When the cause is unknown, use an honest loading or error explanation instead of confidently stating that the account contains no records.

REVIEW THE WORDS IN A TRANSITION

Enter a zero-result query, change it and return after data becomes available. Check that the explanation updates with the state and that the recovery action does not discard useful input. Review how the result is announced without forcing unnecessary focus movement.

This guide focuses on the copy and action for one observed state. For product-wide consistency, classify the causes first; for implementation acceptance, test persistence and recovery separately.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

EMPTY STATES IN SAAS DASHBOARDS SHOULD EXPLAIN THE NEXT STEP
EMPTY STATES IN SAAS DASHBOARDS SHOULD EXPLAIN THE NEXT STEP

A product needs an empty-state model before it needs an empty-state component. Visually similar panels can represent different responsibilities and different risks.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-06-30
Updated 4 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Use two axes: cause and agency
Create a small taxonomy
Make classification part of the component API
Review adjacent states together
Keep an inventory with named owners
Keep access denial out of the no-results bucket
USE TWO AXES: CAUSE AND AGENCY

First identify why the surface is empty. Then identify who can change that situation: the current user, another person, a background process or nobody within the product. The combination gives the design a more useful starting point than a generic list of empty-screen layouts.

A first-use state with an enabled creation action is different from the same first-use state shown to a read-only role. The visible absence may be identical, but the available continuation is not.

CREATE A SMALL TAXONOMY
Create a small taxonomy
Cause	What needs explanation	Agency
First use	What belongs here and how it arrives	Creator or administrator
Filtered result	Which conditions produced no matches	Current user
Incomplete setup	What prerequisite is missing	Setup owner
Permission	What may safely be disclosed	Access owner
Synchronization	Whether the result is still pending	System or integration
Failure	What is known and what remains intact	User, support or system
MAKE CLASSIFICATION PART OF THE COMPONENT API

A reusable component needs enough inputs to express a meaningful state: title, explanation, optional context and an appropriate action. It should not force every cause into the same primary button or celebratory visual.

Keep authorization and data fetching outside the presentational component. A UI variant can represent a permission state, but it cannot decide whether a person is entitled to see a record. That decision belongs to the product's actual access model.

REVIEW ADJACENT STATES TOGETHER

Place loading, loaded, empty, stale and failed states beside each other during design review. Ask whether they can be distinguished without relying on color. A delayed synchronization should not briefly look like an authoritative statement that no data exists.

Also review how the state changes after a successful action. If a new record arrives, the empty message should give way to the relevant content. If another person must act first, the interface should preserve the explanation rather than offering a misleading retry loop.

KEEP AN INVENTORY WITH NAMED OWNERS

For each module, record the cause, role, source of truth, recovery action and open question. This exposes places where a visually shared pattern masks different business rules. It also helps the team identify which parts of the model can be reused and which need an exception.

This is a product-wide classification exercise, not the short copywriting task covered by the focused empty-state guide. A consistent taxonomy makes the component useful because the team understands what each variant means.

KEEP ACCESS DENIAL OUT OF THE NO-RESULTS BUCKET

The piHub source gives access denial its own screen. That distinction matters: no matching products and no permission to view a page can both remove records from sight, but they need different explanations and different recovery.

The artifact supports a taxonomy discussion. It does not prove who should receive the state or that the server applies the rule correctly.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

HOW TO DESIGN TRANSACTION REVIEW SCREENS FOR CRYPTO APPS
HOW TO DESIGN TRANSACTION REVIEW SCREENS FOR CRYPTO APPS

A transaction review should help someone understand the change they are about to authorize. It should also be honest about what the product can and cannot establish before submission.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Updated 4 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Lead with the proposed change
Distinguish selection from signing
Keep the result model more precise than a spinner
Do not generalize technical outcomes across networks
Test uncertainty before writing reassurance
Inspect a result panel without calling it authorization
LEAD WITH THE PROPOSED CHANGE

Explain the action in product language, then provide the details needed to inspect it: destination, asset, amount and relevant cost or consequence when the integration can establish them. Keep uncertainty visible instead of presenting an estimate as a guarantee.

The review is a decision point. It should be possible to return and correct the intent before authorization. A primary button that says only Continue can be weaker than a label that explains the actual next boundary.

DISTINGUISH SELECTION FROM SIGNING

The reviewed Yarsha token-selection screen identifies the asset before any later transaction review. It is useful evidence of that earlier step. It is not itself a transaction confirmation screen, and I do not relabel it as one.

A source-backed case should keep those stages distinct. Selecting an asset, reviewing an operation, approving a wallet request and observing a result are different events even when the product makes them feel connected.

KEEP THE RESULT MODEL MORE PRECISE THAN A SPINNER
Keep the result model more precise than a spinner
Moment	Question the interface should answer
Before authorization	What change am I being asked to approve?
Wallet handoff	What is the product waiting for?
Submitted	What evidence of submission is available?
Pending or unresolved	What is known, and should I wait or investigate?
Rejected or failed	Did I decline, or did the operation fail?
Resolved	What result is established and where can I inspect it?
DO NOT GENERALIZE TECHNICAL OUTCOMES ACROSS NETWORKS

The actual transaction model belongs to the chosen network and integration. For example, Solana's documentation describes transactions as instructions processed together, with state changes reverted if an instruction fails. That is technical context, not a reason for the UI to promise that every failure has no cost or no consequence.

Have engineering define the evidence available at each stage. A design should not announce a confirmed result merely because the wallet window closed.

Solana transaction documentation
TEST UNCERTAINTY BEFORE WRITING REASSURANCE

Exercise a declined request, delayed confirmation, interrupted return and unknown outcome. Decide what can safely be retried and when the person should inspect the original operation first. Preserve the original intent so recovery does not depend on memory.

This is interface design guidance, not financial or security assurance. The review needs technical verification and appropriate domain input before it can be described as a reliable transaction flow.

INSPECT A RESULT PANEL WITHOUT CALLING IT AUTHORIZATION

The Yarsha detail panel separates spent and received assets from destination and fee. The complete frame in the Yarsha case retains the original dummy values and address. It is a result-detail design, not the screen where a person approves a wallet request.

The source explorer wording also needs chain-specific review. Check the supported network, link destination and result evidence before using that action to reassure someone that an operation is confirmed.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

WEB3 WALLET CONNECTION UX THAT BUILDS TRUST
WEB3 WALLET CONNECTION UX THAT BUILDS TRUST

Wallet connection should answer why the wallet is needed, what is being requested and how to continue if the person declines or cannot connect.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-07-04
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Explain the purpose before opening the wallet
Distinguish connection from the next authorization
Design the recovery branches
Preserve the task across the external handoff
Write acceptance criteria for actual behavior
Keep the evidence boundary clear
EXPLAIN THE PURPOSE BEFORE OPENING THE WALLET

Connect wallet is an action label, not a complete explanation. State what connecting enables in this product and whether useful exploration remains possible without it. Ask at the point the task needs the connection rather than using it as an unexplained gate.

Keep the explanation proportional. A short purpose statement can be enough for a familiar task, while a new or consequential permission needs more context. The exact request should match what the integration actually asks for.

DISTINGUISH CONNECTION FROM THE NEXT AUTHORIZATION

A connection step and a later request to sign or approve an action are separate moments in the interface. Do not make the first seem to grant blanket consent to every subsequent operation. Explain the later request in the context of the action that caused it.

Work with engineering to identify which wallet capabilities and network conditions are genuinely supported. Do not infer support from a generic wallet icon or a selectable provider in a design file.

DESIGN THE RECOVERY BRANCHES
Design the recovery branches
Condition	Useful explanation or next step
User declines	Acknowledge the choice and preserve the original task
No supported wallet	Explain the supported route without impersonating a provider
Unsupported network	Name the requirement and let the person inspect it
Connection interrupted	Explain what is known and whether retry is appropriate
Session no longer available	Ask for reconnection at the relevant task boundary
PRESERVE THE TASK ACROSS THE EXTERNAL HANDOFF

Returning from a wallet should not leave the person unsure why they connected. Keep the originating item, conversation or operation available. If the next action is still required, show it explicitly instead of treating connection as task completion.

Review the mobile path as well as the desktop extension path. A change of app, a closed window and a delayed return can produce different implementation conditions. A prototype alone cannot verify them.

WRITE ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA FOR ACTUAL BEHAVIOR
The reason for connecting is understandable before the request.
Declining does not silently lose the person's previous context.
An unsupported condition receives a specific, truthful explanation.
Connection completion is distinct from transaction completion.
The relevant action remains usable by keyboard where the web integration supports it.
Returning later produces an understandable session state.
KEEP THE EVIDENCE BOUNDARY CLEAR

Yarsha is a relevant messaging-and-wallet design context in my portfolio, but the currently published exports do not show every connection and recovery branch. Those branches are requirements to test, not outcomes to infer from unrelated screens.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

DESIGNING THE HANDOFFS BETWEEN PEOPLE
DESIGNING THE HANDOFFS BETWEEN PEOPLE

A workflow is only as clear as the moment responsibility changes hands. Three interface examples show how I reason about ownership, waiting and recovery.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-11-04
Updated 4 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

The difficult moment is often between screens
First, make ownership visible before asking for action
Then, design waiting as a legitimate state
Finally, separate progress from completion
The handoff note I want beside the frame
THE DIFFICULT MOMENT IS OFTEN BETWEEN SCREENS

A lead looks qualified. An application looks complete. A delivery looks close to finished. None of those states tells us, by itself, who should act next. When I review an operational workflow, I follow responsibility as carefully as I follow navigation. The useful question is: what can this person decide now, and what information will the next person need?

The examples here come from my portfolio designs for Orkest, piHub and Zapp. I use them to explain design decisions and the questions I would resolve before implementation. They are sample-data design screens, not evidence of measured business results.

FIRST, MAKE OWNERSHIP VISIBLE BEFORE ASKING FOR ACTION

In Orkest, the lead list separates All leads, My leads and Unassigned. That distinction matters before a score or a conversion action: a record without an owner is a different operational problem from an owned record that is not ready. Keeping ownership near search and filters makes it part of the working context.

The trade-off is density. Adding every signal to the list would make comparison harder. I would keep the list focused on triage, then use the detail view for the supporting information needed to convert. A useful review task is to ask someone to find a qualified but unassigned lead and explain what they would do next. That is an evaluation proposal, not a result from a completed study.

Orkest leads workspace with summary cards, ownership views, search, filters and the complete record table. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

THEN, DESIGN WAITING AS A LEGITIMATE STATE

The piHub creditor view shows Approved and Awaiting Approval as written statuses. In a workflow that crosses creditor, investor and administrator roles, waiting is part of the product. A person should be able to distinguish a submitted application from a draft without guessing from a colored badge.

The screenshot establishes the comparison view; it does not settle the notification rules. Before handoff, I would specify who can change each status, what explanation accompanies a rejection, and where the creditor returns to correct information. The design responsibility is to make those transitions explicit rather than hiding them behind a generic success message.

PiHub creditor application list keeps service, industry, dates, amounts and written approval status together. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

FINALLY, SEPARATE PROGRESS FROM COMPLETION

Zapp has a driver next-stop screen and a separate delivery-completion screen. That separation creates a useful boundary: arriving near an address and finishing a delivery are different events. The customer and driver need compatible accounts of what has happened, even though they see different interfaces.

I would document what counts as completion, what the driver can do when the recipient is unavailable, and what evidence is retained if the network fails. A completion animation cannot answer those questions. The next-stop design below is a starting point for specifying them.

Zapp driver screen distinguishes a confirmed pickup from the next drop-off and offers arrival and intermediate-stop issue actions. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

THE HANDOFF NOTE I WANT BESIDE THE FRAME

I finish this kind of review with a short behavior contract. It records the current owner, permitted action, information carried forward, next owner and recovery path. If the team cannot agree on one of those, another polished screen is unlikely to resolve the ambiguity.

The journey is complete when a reader can explain the next decision and its consequences. In a portfolio, that means showing enough of the original screen to preserve context, explaining the trade-off, and being clear about what still needs validation.

Name the role that owns the next action.
Show whether the item is editable, submitted, waiting or complete.
Specify what persists when the transition fails.
Test the transition across roles, not only each screen in isolation.

ABOUT NISCHHAL RAJ SUBBA
I DESIGN BY STAYING CLOSE TO THE PRODUCT AND CLOSE TO THE BUILD.
I DESIGN BY STAYING CLOSE TO THE PRODUCT AND CLOSE TO THE BUILD.

I’m a Nepal-based product designer working remotely. My work spans UX architecture, interface design, design systems, technical websites and implementation handoff.

I started in agency and client work, which taught me to move between industries and explain design decisions to people with very different priorities. Product roles pushed the work deeper: more states, longer-lived systems, permissions, data, engineering constraints and the consequences of decisions that cannot be solved by a nicer component.

That is the part of design I enjoy most. I like products where the brief is incomplete and the interface has to make a complicated system easier to reason about. I care about hierarchy, state language, recovery, responsive behavior and the quiet rules that make a product feel predictable.

I also stay close to implementation. I do not need to own the front end on every project, but understanding browser behavior, component constraints and UI QA makes my design work more practical and my handoff less theatrical.

A SHORT EXPLANATION OF WHAT THIS PORTFOLIO COLLECTS.
A SHORT EXPLANATION OF WHAT THIS PORTFOLIO COLLECTS.

This site exists to show my work and let people contact me. I do not sell personal information or build advertising profiles from portfolio visitors.

01 · CONTACT FORM
WHAT YOU SEND

If you use the contact form, I receive the information you enter, such as your name, email address, inquiry type, timeline and message. The form may also include the page you submitted from and the submission time so the inquiry has useful context.

Please do not send passwords, account credentials, sensitive financial information, medical information or anything else that does not belong in an ordinary professional email.

02 · PURPOSE
HOW I USE IT

I use contact details to reply to job opportunities, project inquiries, portfolio questions or professional collaborations. Messages may remain in my email history so a conversation can continue and I can keep a reasonable record of professional correspondence.

03 · SITE MEASUREMENT
ANALYTICS

The site may use limited analytics or interaction events to understand whether pages, project links and contact actions are working as intended. I do not use portfolio analytics to create third-party advertising audiences.

LINKS LEAVE THIS PORTFOLIO

Links to services such as LinkedIn, Behance, GitHub, Uxcel or external project material are governed by those services once you leave this site.

CORRECTION OR DELETION

If you want information you previously sent corrected or deleted, email hinischalsubba@gmail.com. Include enough context for me to identify the relevant message.

WHEN THIS NOTICE CHANGES

I update this page when the contact provider, analytics setup or site architecture changes in a way that affects how visitor information is handled. Last reviewed: August 2026.

HOW FINDINGS BECOME A FIX PLAN

Each finding should identify the route and task, reproduction steps, expected and observed behavior, supporting evidence and a test for the fix.

Priority follows the consequence: a blocked core task or unsafe action needs attention before a recoverable delay; a cosmetic inconsistency comes later. Frequency, affected users and available workarounds can change that order.

For example, a failed submission that discards the message is more urgent than inconsistent spacing. The report should make that distinction explicit so the team can choose what to fix first.

text:
MOBILE · WEB3 MESSAGING AND WALLET CONTEXT

YARSHA
YARSHA

Keeping contact, asset selection and consequential actions understandable inside a conversational product.

CONTRIBUTION
Product design contribution
EVIDENCE
Complete original Figma screens · sample design content

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN A FAMILIAR CONVERSATION BECOME THE STARTING POINT FOR WEB3 ACTIONS WITHOUT MAKING EVERY ACTION FEEL EQUALLY CASUAL?

The journey begins with a person, not a wallet balance. A contact becomes a conversation; that conversation can lead to shared content, a group or an asset-related action. I organized the case around the moments when the interface needs to preserve familiarity and the moments when it needs to ask for more attention.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Find and recognize a person
Build context in conversation
Choose the recipient and asset
Organize a shared group
Inspect the transaction detail
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

Yarsha brings a contact directory, conversation, shared groups and wallet-related actions into one mobile product. Those activities can begin with the same person but require different levels of attention. Finding a friend is lightweight; choosing an asset or inspecting a transaction needs a more deliberate check.

My product-design contribution focused on how those surfaces connect: identity before conversation, context before action, and a clear place to return. The following walkthrough uses complete frames from the supplied Final Mobile Design page. It follows the designed experience rather than claiming that these frames document a research timeline or a shipped financial service.

Constraints that shaped the work
Wallet and network behavior extends beyond the messaging interface.
Asset labels and transaction context must remain distinguishable from decorative chat content.
Contacts, balances and identifiers in a design file may be sensitive even when they are sample content.
01 / FIND AND RECOGNIZE A PERSON

Before any conversation or transfer, the person needs confidence that they have found the right contact.

START WITH RECOGNITION, THEN HANDLE THE MISS

The directory pairs display names with shortened wallet identifiers. A name helps recognition; the identifier distinguishes people whose names or avatars may be similar. Search and the add-contact action sit inside the same contact model instead of sending the person into an unrelated wallet screen.

The empty-result state is part of that first step. The query and keyboard remain visible while Contacts and Invite offer different routes forward. That preserves the effort already made, but it also exposes a decision to resolve: when should the product suggest revising a query, adding someone or inviting them?

Open image ↗

Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
Familiar names reduce effort, while wallet precision and explicit recovery prevent familiarity from becoming ambiguity.

02 / BUILD CONTEXT IN CONVERSATION

After recognition, the product can shift from finding someone to understanding the relationship.

KEEP A CONVERSATION CONNECTED TO ITS IDENTITY AND HISTORY

The conversation keeps the contact identity in its header and the composer at the bottom, leaving the middle for shared history. The profile then gives that identity more depth through a wallet address, media, groups and links. These surfaces give different answers to the same question: who am I interacting with?

In-thread search adds a second way to recover context. It retains the conversation and provides a match count with previous and next controls. A person looking for an earlier link should not have to abandon the thread and reconstruct the search elsewhere.

TRADE-OFF
A familiar chat layout supports continuity, but profile and search details must remain reachable without crowding the primary conversation.

03 / CHOOSE THE RECIPIENT AND ASSET

The familiar social context now gives way to a decision that needs greater precision.

CHANGE THE PACE WHEN THE ACTION CONCERNS AN ASSET

Send Money begins with a username or wallet-address search and recognizable contacts. Asset selection then separates tokens from NFTs. That order makes the recipient and the asset distinct decisions rather than compressing everything into a single ambiguous action.

Tokens use names, symbols and balance-like sample values; NFT collections use artwork and collection names. The visual treatment follows the object being selected. Before authorization, the implementation still needs a review that reconciles recipient, network, asset and amount, including unavailable assets and similarly named items.

TRADE-OFF
Different asset types need different selection patterns, while a shared review model must preserve the identity and consequence of the action.

04 / ORGANIZE A SHARED GROUP

A relationship can expand from one person into a shared space with its own responsibilities.

MAKE MEMBERSHIP AND SHARING UNDERSTANDABLE

Group creation starts with member selection. The detail screen then exposes the group identity, description and member roles alongside shared-content tabs. The interface changes from choosing participants to understanding the space they now share.

The invitation screen isolates the link and provides Copy and Share as separate actions. That makes distribution explicit. A complete group model also needs decisions about who can invite, what an invite grants, and how a person understands that access before joining.

Easy sharing helps a group grow; explicit roles and invitation scope keep membership understandable.

05 / INSPECT THE TRANSACTION DETAIL

The story ends with a detail view someone can return to and question.

GIVE THE CONSEQUENTIAL ACTION AN INSPECTABLE RECORD

The transaction-detail frame separates spent and received assets from the destination and network fee. An explorer action provides a route beyond the in-app summary. The hierarchy should help a person connect the summary to the underlying event rather than merely display a success-looking card.

The original frame contains a Blastscan label within a Solana-oriented design context. I retain that source detail rather than silently correcting the screenshot. It is a concrete handoff issue: the intended network, explorer destination and pending or rejected states need to agree before implementation.

Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
A concise summary is useful only when its destination, network and evidence remain traceable.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

Twelve complete original frames make the designed path inspectable from contact discovery through conversation, asset selection, group membership and transaction detail. Dummy content is shown unchanged under the owner’s publication authorization. Wallet authorization, transaction execution and cross-device state remain integration work.

Open Yarsha design
WHERE THE WORK LANDED

The design account now exposes the relationships between the app’s social and financial surfaces. The strongest questions are continuity questions: whether the person, asset and group context remain clear at the handoff between screens. No adoption or transaction-performance measurement is reported.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask someone to detect an incorrect recipient, asset or network before authorizing a transfer.
Exercise rejection, a delayed confirmation and returning from an explorer. Check whether retrying could accidentally duplicate the action.
Looking back

The system works as a relationship between surfaces: names help recognition, wallet identifiers add precision, and review states explain consequence. The most useful consistency is not identical layout everywhere. It is being able to move between these contexts without losing who or what the action concerns.

WEB3 PROTOCOL · WEBSITE COMMUNICATION

MOKSHYA.IO
MOKSHYA.IO

A technical product story with an accessible first explanation and a deeper path for people evaluating the mechanism.

CONTRIBUTION

EVIDENCE
Existing portfolio material; original screen evidence incomplete

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN A PROTOCOL WEBSITE EXPLAIN ENOUGH FOR A NEWCOMER WITHOUT FRUSTRATING A TECHNICAL EVALUATOR?

The website has to introduce an idea before it can ask someone to evaluate a mechanism. My approach connects the opening proposition to deeper technical reading, then keeps explanation and proof together as the layout changes. This case follows that reading path within my website design contribution.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Establish relevance
Expose the mechanism
Keep proof beside the claim
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

Mokshya's website needs to serve visitors with different levels of technical knowledge. Someone encountering the product for the first time needs a useful mental model. A developer or evaluator needs enough specificity to investigate further. My contribution centered on information architecture, section sequence and responsive composition.

This case is about protocol-product communication on the website. It should not be read as proof that I designed a complete wallet, implemented the protocol or verified financial outcomes. The existing website preview provides visual context for this contribution.

Constraints that shaped the work
The first explanation must be readable without removing the technical distinctions that matter.
Claims need nearby supporting material rather than generic trust language.
Long sections must keep their reading order and relationship to evidence on smaller screens.
01 / ESTABLISH RELEVANCE

Start with the reason a visitor should care.

LET THE OUTCOME ESTABLISH RELEVANCE

I structure the opening around what the product makes possible before asking the visitor to learn its terminology. That gives technical detail a purpose: it answers a question the page has already helped the visitor form.

The trade-off is precision. A short statement should narrow the claim rather than replace an explanation with a sweeping Web3 promise. Where the mechanism matters, the next section must supply it.

TRADE-OFF
Plain language lowers the entry barrier; narrowing the claim preserves technical precision.

02 / EXPOSE THE MECHANISM

Relevance creates the next question: how does this actually work?

CONNECT THE SUMMARY TO DEEPER EVALUATION

An introductory path and a developer path can share one coherent story without requiring the same reading depth. The summary explains the proposition; deeper material exposes the mechanism and the evidence available to inspect.

This is a content-hierarchy decision rather than a measured finding about visitor behavior. I would test whether a newcomer can explain the offer and whether a technical evaluator can find the detail they need without reading the entire page.

TRADE-OFF
Progressive depth accommodates different readers without forcing everyone through the longest explanation.

03 / KEEP PROOF BESIDE THE CLAIM

The explanation only holds together when its supporting material remains nearby.

PRESERVE EXPLANATION AND PROOF AS A PAIR

A supporting artifact is most useful near the statement it helps assess. On mobile, I keep that relationship in the reading order instead of letting a desktop column arrangement separate the explanation from its supporting visual.

That requires reviewing actual headings, paragraph lengths and image behavior at narrow widths. A responsive page can fit the viewport while still telling its story in an unhelpful order.

TRADE-OFF
A responsive rearrangement must preserve meaning as well as fit the viewport.

EXISTING PORTFOLIO PREVIEW
Open image ↗

Retained portfolio presentation. A matching original Figma screen has not been verified for this case.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

The portfolio scope is the website's narrative structure, responsive hierarchy and interface composition. The retained website preview provides context; the contribution described here is the narrative structure and interface composition.

Public material for this case is limited. This account stays focused on my contribution, its design decisions and the questions that deserve further validation.

WHERE THE WORK LANDED

The website account focuses on the order of explanation: establish relevance, then expose the technical mechanism. A first-impression task and a developer-information retrieval task would test those two reading paths. The available material does not include a measured comprehension result.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask a newcomer to explain the protocol’s purpose after the opening, then find the route to deeper technical information.
Ask a technical evaluator to locate the evidence behind a capability claim without repeatedly returning to the top-level introduction.
Looking back

Each layer should answer the question raised by the previous one. A newcomer and a developer can share the opening without needing the same depth. The strongest editorial structure makes the next useful question easy to pursue.

SOFTWARE STUDIO · BRAND, WEBSITE AND FRONTEND

HAMRO IDEA
HAMRO IDEA

Connecting a Nepal-based studio's positioning, services, project proof and contact path in one maintainable website.

CONTRIBUTION
Design and development contribution
EVIDENCE
Complete original Figma screens · sample design content

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN A SOFTWARE STUDIO MAKE ITS OFFER UNDERSTANDABLE AND GIVE A PROSPECT A REASON TO BELIEVE IT?

The website needs to connect three things that often drift apart: what the studio offers, which work supports that offer, and how a prospect starts a relevant conversation. My design and development contribution brings them into one reading path and a reusable frontend structure.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Choose a relevant service
Inspect the work and studio
Explore the studio’s thinking
Start a relevant conversation
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

Hamro Idea needed a website that could explain a software studio's offer to a prospective client. The first design question was what a visitor should understand before making contact, not which visual treatment would make the homepage more dramatic.

My existing scope spans positioning, information architecture, responsive UI, reusable sections, semantic markup and frontend implementation. Working across design and code let me inspect the page with real content and adjust its composition before treating the layout as finished.

Constraints that shaped the work
Internal service names may not match the language a prospective client uses.
A multi-page site needs repeated patterns without making every service sound identical.
The design must tolerate real copy, image proportions and future content changes.
01 / CHOOSE A RELEVANT SERVICE

The prospect first needs to recognize a service that fits the problem.

ORGANIZE THE OFFER AROUND CLIENT QUESTIONS

I structure a service page around fit: what problem the service addresses, what work it includes and what proof helps someone evaluate it. That makes the service architecture more useful than a list of internal disciplines.

The practical editorial test is whether a prospect can select a relevant service and explain why it fits. That is a proposed test, not a claim about measured lead quality.

The complete homepage and services page reveal how the offer is introduced and then expanded. These are historical design artifacts with placeholder imagery and copy; their value here is the information sequence, not the sample business claims.

02 / INSPECT THE WORK AND STUDIO

A relevant service creates a reasonable demand for evidence.

KEEP PROJECT PROOF NEAR THE SERVICE EXPLANATION

The project index offers a first scan of work, and the project-detail layout gives one example room for explanation. The About page answers a related trust question about the studio behind that work. These are different kinds of proof and should not compete as an undifferentiated gallery.

The About page gives a prospective client another way to evaluate the studio after reading the service offer. Positioning, team presentation and working principles should support the promise made by the earlier pages rather than introduce a disconnected brand story.

I treat that transition as a trust question: what does the visitor still need to understand before starting a conversation? The source contains demonstration imagery and sample claims, so the case discusses their placement and role without presenting them as verified company achievements.

03 / EXPLORE THE STUDIO’S THINKING

A visitor may want to understand the studio’s thinking before starting a project conversation.

GIVE A CURIOUS VISITOR ANOTHER WAY TO GO DEEPER

The article index and long-form article layout create that optional route. A short preview helps someone decide what is worth opening; the article page then needs a clear reading hierarchy and a useful route back to related material.

I treat editorial content as part of evaluation, not filler between services and contact. In these historical designs the article text and project claims are sample content; the inspectable decision is how the index, detail and next step connect.

04 / START A RELEVANT CONVERSATION

After understanding the offer and inspecting relevant work, the prospect needs a clear route to a conversation.

MAKE THE NEXT CONVERSATION EASY TO START

The full contact page brings that evaluation path into a direct request. Name, email and message keep the initial commitment small, while the broader page retains the studio identity and surrounding navigation. The original placeholder content remains visible as part of the historical design.

The artifact also exposes work still needed: prompts must become persistent programmatic labels, the email field needs appropriate input semantics, and validation, submission progress and success feedback need explicit states. Preserving the simple composition requires making those behaviors part of the implementation contract.

A short form reduces the information requested upfront, while qualification and useful feedback still need a deliberate interaction design.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

The work joins service information architecture with a static multi-page frontend. The useful handoff is not only a visual style: it includes section responsibilities, responsive rules and a content structure the site can keep using.

Public material for this case is limited. This account stays focused on my contribution, its design decisions and the questions that deserve further validation.

WHERE THE WORK LANDED

The contribution joins service structure, project proof and a maintainable frontend. I would evaluate it by asking a visitor to choose a service, locate supporting work and reach contact with the right context. Search rankings and inquiry growth are not measured outcomes of this case.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask a prospect to choose a relevant service, locate supporting work and reach contact with enough context to describe their need.
Review the form using keyboard input, invalid email, submission failure and success; check persistent labels and meaningful feedback.
Looking back

Service architecture and implementation meet in the content contract. A new service or longer project description should fit the structure without weakening the story. The case demonstrates the intended relationship between offer, proof and contact; lead quality and search growth need separate measurement.

text:
B2B CONSULTING · SERVICE AND SECTOR WEBSITE

MORAJAA
MORAJAA

Helping a prospective client move from a recognizable business problem to a specific consulting service and a useful conversation.

CONTRIBUTION
UX, content structure and website design contribution
EVIDENCE
Complete original Figma screens · sample design content

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN A VISITOR EVALUATE A COMPLEX CONSULTING ENGAGEMENT BEFORE SPEAKING TO SALES?

The useful journey begins with a business situation, not with the consultancy’s service taxonomy. I connected the page sequence around three questions: is this relevant to me, what does the engagement involve, and where can I go next? The complete homepage, service and sector pages show that progression at three levels of detail.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Recognize the service fit
Understand the engagement
Choose a relevant next path
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

Morajaa presents consulting services and sectors to visitors who may know their business problem before they know the consultancy's terminology. My contribution covered information architecture, service and sector page structure, responsive composition and inquiry paths.

The source for this case is the supplied Final Design v2 page. The reviewed example comes from the Market Entry in Saudi Arabia service design. It is a design artifact, not independent verification of the consultancy's legal claims, service performance or client results.

Constraints that shaped the work
Service and sector categories need to connect without making visitors read duplicate pages.
Long-form explanation must remain scannable without reducing an involved service to a slogan.
A page should communicate the consultancy's scope without turning the portfolio into a source of regulatory advice.
01 / RECOGNIZE THE SERVICE FIT

The opening needs to earn attention by making the service recognizable.

MAKE THE SERVICE CONCRETE BEFORE ASKING FOR AN INQUIRY

A consulting category becomes more useful when a visitor can see the work involved. The market-entry design moves from an introduction into setup services, ongoing support and a named process. That sequence gives the call to action more context than a standalone contact button.

My editorial priority is the relationship between those sections. The first scan should establish relevance; deeper reading should explain the scope and sequence well enough to support a more informed inquiry.

The complete homepage gives this opening its wider context: the service offer, sector content and routes to deeper evaluation are part of one reading path.

TRADE-OFF
A concise introduction helps scanning but must lead into service depth rather than replace it.

02 / UNDERSTAND THE ENGAGEMENT

Once relevance is established, the visitor needs a more concrete picture of the work.

USE A PROCESS SECTION TO REVEAL THE SHAPE OF THE ENGAGEMENT

The source design breaks the process into named stages, including entry planning, sector feasibility and operationalization. The stage titles carry the scan; supporting text supplies detail. A visitor can inspect the structure before committing to reading every paragraph.

The complete service page shows how the process connects to the opening, capabilities, imagery and contact path. The consultancy's process wording is shown as source content; the portfolio does not endorse it as legal or regulatory guidance.

The service pages offer alternative routes rather than a sequence every visitor must complete. Joint ventures, tender management and HR outsourcing reuse the same broad reading rhythm while changing the scope, benefits and engagement detail. The design question is whether someone can recognize the relevant offer without learning a new page structure each time.

03 / CHOOSE A RELEVANT NEXT PATH

ALLOW MORE THAN ONE SENSIBLE ENTRY PATH

Services describe the kind of support offered, while sectors describe the visitor's operating context. Both can be useful routes into the same business. The design task is to connect them without forcing one taxonomy to stand in for the other.

On smaller screens, that relationship needs descriptive links and a deliberate reading order. Stacking a desktop layout is not enough if the explanation and its supporting action become separated.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Looking back

text:
FINTECH · CREDITOR, INVESTOR AND ADMINISTRATOR JOURNEYS

PIHUB
PIHUB

Financial workflows organized around what has been submitted, who needs to act and what remains unresolved.

CONTRIBUTION
Product design contribution
EVIDENCE
Complete original Figma screens · sample design content

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW DOES A FINANCIAL WORKFLOW REMAIN UNDERSTANDABLE WHEN THE NEXT STEP BELONGS TO ANOTHER PERSON?

For piHub, the journey is not a straight line from application to approval. It crosses creditor, investor and administrator roles, and includes legitimate waiting. I organized the case around that handover: make the current state visible, keep each role’s job distinct, and explain what happens when a person cannot continue.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Understand the application
Change role without changing meaning
Recover at the access boundary
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

piHub spans creditor, investor and administrative experiences. The recurring interaction problem is uncertainty: a person may have supplied information but still be waiting on verification, review or another party. A short status label is useful only when its meaning and the next available action are clear.

My existing portfolio scope covers applications, credit requests, verification, account management and dashboards. I worked on information hierarchy, forms, state language and the relationship between a process state and the action available to each role. The role prototypes are separate artifacts; they do not constitute a synchronized financial application.

Constraints that shaped the work
The same financial process is viewed by people with different tasks and permissions.
Application data and sample financial values must not be mistaken for verified transactions or product results.
A process can legitimately require waiting; the interface must explain that boundary rather than invent progress.
01 / UNDERSTAND THE APPLICATION

The creditor’s first need is an overview of what has already been submitted.

KEEP APPLICATION STATE IN THE COMPARISON VIEW

The creditor journey starts with company information, moves into a product application and returns to a list of submitted work. Each screen answers a different question: who is applying, what is being requested and what happens next.

Keeping written status alongside service, industry, dates and amounts lets someone compare applications without opening every record. The complete screens retain their original dummy values so the hierarchy can be judged in context.

02 / CHANGE ROLE WITHOUT CHANGING MEANING

That view is only one side of the process. Investor priorities require a different object and information hierarchy.

SHARE STATUS LANGUAGE WITHOUT FLATTENING THE ROLES

The investor side changes the job. Account entry leads into defining an offer, comparing products and reviewing incoming credit requests. Reusing the creditor’s exact information hierarchy would hide that difference in responsibility.

The connection between roles is the state model, not an identical table. A review should follow one application across those surfaces and check that Submitted, Reviewing and Approved mean the same event while each role sees the information it needs.

TRADE-OFF
Consistent status language supports cross-role understanding; identical columns would obscure the different jobs.

03 / RECOVER AT THE ACCESS BOUNDARY

The journey also needs a boundary: some actions or records are not available to the current account.

GIVE REVIEW AND RECOVERY THEIR OWN REQUIREMENTS

A verification request should say what information needs attention and preserve what is already valid. A waiting state should identify the dependency when that information can safely be disclosed. An error should distinguish a correctable input problem from a service interruption.

Those are acceptance conditions for the workflow, not financial promises. They make the handoff discussion more useful than a blanket requirement to make the onboarding shorter.

The administrator source also contains an access-denied design with a Go Back action. That is a proposed recovery surface. The account and server still need to decide whether a direct request is allowed; an error screen does not establish that enforcement.

PiHub administrator access-denied screen gives the person an explanation and a Go Back action. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
Recovery copy should be useful without exposing restricted record details.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

I organize the discussion around role, current state, outstanding requirement and next action. The linked creditor, investor and admin prototypes provide paths for inspecting the design. Production permissions, uploads, persistence and real financial processing require separate engineering verification.

Open creditor prototype
Open investor prototype
Open admin prototype
Creditor prototype
Investor prototype
Admin prototype
WHERE THE WORK LANDED

The role split is visible in the artifacts: creditors submit applications, investors manage products and requests, and administrators review access and records. The remaining evaluation is whether the same status has a consistent meaning across those roles and whether a person knows who must act next.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask a creditor to identify who owns the next step after submission and what would require a response.
Trace an application returned for changes across creditor, investor and administrator views; check that their status language describes the same event.
Looking back

The state model is part of the product experience. A shorter form cannot compensate for a person who has submitted information and no longer understands who is responsible. The next evaluation should trace one application across the role boundaries, including a request for changes.

text:
WORDPRESS LMS · COLLABORATIVE PRODUCT DESIGN

MASTERIYO
MASTERIYO

Designing authoring and learning interactions inside an established LMS, while keeping the contribution boundary clear.

CONTRIBUTION
Product UI and UX contribution within a team
EVIDENCE
Complete original Figma screens · sample design content

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW DO YOU HELP A COURSE AUTHOR BUILD SOMETHING COMPLEX WITHOUT MAKING EVERY CONFIGURATION DECISION COMPETE AT ONCE?

The authoring journey starts with a blank course, grows into an outline, then narrows into a quiz and its questions. My contribution sits within Masteriyo’s wider product team. The screens below let the case follow that growing complexity while showing how repeated patterns maintain orientation.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Create the first content
Build the course outline
Set up an assessment
Configure a question
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

Masteriyo brings course creation and learning into an established WordPress LMS. A creator organizes sections, lessons and assessments; a learner encounters the resulting sequence. My product UI and UX contribution was part of the wider team’s work, including course and quiz flows and reusable interaction patterns.

This case follows the authoring side through four screens from the supplied primary file. They are team design artifacts that I have permission to present with attribution. They do not establish sole authorship of the product, or measured changes in learner completion.

Constraints that shaped the work
Work within an existing WordPress LMS and the wider product team’s conventions.
Expose different levels of content without confusing course structure with question configuration.
Keep the team contribution explicit and treat save, scoring and keyboard behavior as implementation requirements.
01 / CREATE THE FIRST CONTENT

An empty course is the first authoring task, not a dead end.

MAKE A BLANK COURSE ACTIONABLE

The empty builder offers Add Section, Add Assignment and Add Quiz, with documentation below. Rather than describing an absence, it gives the author concrete ways to begin. The design places help beside creation without making documentation a prerequisite.

The unresolved hierarchy is worth examining: the three actions have equal visual weight even though a section and an assessment belong to different levels of the content model. A first-use review should establish whether authors know which one to choose.

Course title and description give the object an identity before the empty builder asks the author to add content. Together, the frames show a transition from defining a course to making its first structural decision.

Masteriyo course creation starts with a course title and description before content building. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

Masteriyo empty course builder offers Add Section, Add Assignment and Add Quiz, with a separate documentation link. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
Several creation routes expose capability, but equally weighted buttons leave authors to choose the appropriate starting unit.

02 / BUILD THE COURSE OUTLINE

Once content exists, the interface must explain how it belongs together.

LET THE OUTLINE CARRY THE COURSE STRUCTURE

The populated builder groups lesson rows inside an Introduction section. A section-level menu and collapse control are separate from each lesson’s edit, duplicate and delete actions. Add New Content stays inside the group; Add New Section sits outside it. That spatial distinction communicates the parent-child relationship.

Reordering is visible through drag handles, but the design still needs a keyboard alternative and meaningful names for compact actions. The header also shows Course selected while the screen contains builder content; that active-state inconsistency belongs in the implementation review.

Section and lesson editors then reveal the next levels of detail. The outline remains the organizing model while the fields change to suit the selected object. That relationship is more useful than forcing every editor into an identical form.

Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
Compact row actions preserve a readable outline; their icons need names, focus states and safe destructive behavior in implementation.

03 / SET UP AN ASSESSMENT

A quiz adds a different configuration task inside that course structure.

INTRODUCE QUIZ COMPLEXITY IN STAGES

Quiz setup separates Info, Questions and Settings. The first surface asks for a name and description and provides Next and Cancel. It establishes the assessment before introducing the denser work of writing and configuring questions.

The sequence needs an explicit state contract: what Next validates, whether a partially written quiz can be saved, and what Cancel discards. These are requirements for completing the interaction, rather than behaviors proved by a static frame.

Masteriyo Add New Quiz form separates Info, Questions and Settings and offers Next and Cancel actions. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
Tabs break the setup into parts, while each step still needs clear completion and validation rules.

04 / CONFIGURE A QUESTION

Question editing is the deepest level shown here, where configuration density grows quickly.

KEEP QUESTION DETAIL CONNECTED TO ITS PLACE IN THE QUIZ

The question editor keeps the list of questions above the expanded question. Within that editor, question type and points are separate from answer rows. Required and Randomize settings sit below the answers. This gives the author several layers of context without opening an unrelated screen for every adjustment.

For a true-or-false question, the selected correct answer must remain understandable beyond its green treatment. Reorder controls, duplication, deletion and saving need the same interaction conventions as the broader authoring system. That consistency is where a team contribution becomes easier for others to continue.

The multiple-choice example makes the reuse question concrete: question identity and points remain familiar, while the answer configuration changes with question type. The complete frames expose both the shared pattern and the extra density that each type introduces.

Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
Keeping the question list visible supports context, but answer configuration must remain clearly subordinate to the selected question.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

Four authoring states connect a blank course to its outline, quiz setup and question configuration. They are presented as team design work within my contribution to course and quiz UI/UX. The primary file is the source; the older copy remains a separate historical reference. Saving, scoring, accessibility and learner behavior require implementation evidence.

Explore Masteriyo — current product website
Explore the original Masteriyo design file
WHERE THE WORK LANDED

The artifact-backed result is an authoring structure that separates course organization from assessment detail. The screenshots make the hierarchy and its remaining review questions inspectable. No learner-completion, adoption or task-time measurements are available.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask a course author to create a section, add a lesson and configure a quiz without losing their place in the course outline.
Review question reordering, an invalid answer and cancellation with unsaved changes; verify keyboard access and feedback alongside the visual hierarchy.
Looking back

The useful system is a stable relationship between structure and detail. Section, lesson, quiz and answer are different levels, and the interface has to make the current level obvious. The visible tab highlight and icon-only actions also deserve implementation review: source artifacts are valuable because they expose unfinished decisions as well as strong ones.

text:
MOBILE LOGISTICS · CUSTOMER, DRIVER AND OPERATIONS

ZAPP TODAY
ZAPP TODAY

Different interfaces for people booking a delivery, carrying it out and resolving exceptions around it.

CONTRIBUTION
Mobile product design contribution
EVIDENCE
Complete original Figma screens · sample design content

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN THE SAME DELIVERY FEEL CLEAR TO THE PERSON BOOKING IT AND THE PERSON CARRYING IT OUT?

I treated the delivery as a shared lifecycle with different viewpoints. A customer first establishes an account and describes the parcel. A driver later needs the current stop and a clear completion boundary. Reading those moments together reveals the handovers that isolated mobile mockups tend to hide.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Enter as a customer
Describe the parcel
Act on the next stop
Close the handoff
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

A delivery creates shared state but different priorities. A customer needs to prepare a request and understand what happens next. A driver needs a clear operational task. An operations team needs the context required to investigate an exception. My existing project scope covers these related journeys, rather than one app screen in isolation.

This case uses the supplied Zapp 2.0 customer iOS file as its primary visual source. Historical customer and driver prototypes remain separately labeled. I have not combined those older screens with the newer design and presented the result as one approved release.

Constraints that shaped the work
Customer and driver priorities differ even when they refer to the same delivery.
Maps, location, pricing and live tracking require real services; a prototype cannot establish their accuracy.
The current source contains QA and experimental frames, which are withheld from the public illustration set.
01 / ENTER AS A CUSTOMER

Before the delivery request, account entry needs to make the two starting paths understandable.

MAKE ACCOUNT ENTRY AN UNDERSTANDABLE CHOICE

The account-entry frame distinguishes Create account from Sign in and gives each a short explanation. The primary action gives the new-customer path more emphasis without hiding the returning-user route.

That is a narrow but useful decision to inspect. It shows onboarding hierarchy, not evidence that registration became faster or that the full delivery service was implemented.

The complete account sequence shows how that choice leads into registration and code verification. The important continuity is what survives the transition: the entered mobile number, a clear resend route and an explanation of what the next action will do.

Open image ↗

TRADE-OFF
A dominant new-account route helps first-time customers, while returning users still need a visible sign-in path.

02 / DESCRIBE THE PARCEL

After entry, the question becomes what the service needs to know about the item.

ASK FOR PARCEL CONTEXT AT THE POINT IT MATTERS

The parcel-details frame presents Documents, Small parcel and Large parcel with short descriptions, then asks for contents. Its visible step indicator places the task inside a longer request. The action says Choose delivery service, which tells the customer what the next screen is for.

This structure keeps package description separate from the choice of service. Before implementation, the team still needs rules for unsupported items, size limits, edited answers and validation. The screenshot shows the proposed sequence rather than proving those rules exist.

Home gives the request its starting context, parcel details establish what is being carried, and service selection turns that information into a timing choice. Showing these frames together makes the booking sequence visible instead of treating the parcel screen as an isolated form.

TRADE-OFF

03 / ACT ON THE NEXT STOP

The viewpoint now changes from preparing a request to carrying out a stop.

REVIEW ONE LIFECYCLE ACROSS THE ROLE BOUNDARIES

The driver stop-order screen distinguishes a confirmed pickup from the next drop-off. It shows progress and separates arrival from an intermediate-stop issue. The screen explicitly says navigation is inactive in the prototype, so I present it as a proposed task sequence.

This makes a cross-role review more specific: confirm which stop is current, which event changes its state, and what the customer or operations team should see after an issue. Separate screens still need synchronized data and real routing before that lifecycle can be called implemented.

Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
A focused current-stop action supports execution, but exception reporting must remain reachable.

04 / CLOSE THE HANDOFF

The final moment is not simply a success graphic: it must explain which responsibility has ended.

SEPARATE DELIVERY COMPLETION FROM SETTLEMENT

The driver completion frame names the completed handoff, offers a return to availability and states that settlement and earnings require verified server records. Those are different responsibilities, and the completion message keeps them separate.

For acceptance testing, I would check an interrupted handoff, a duplicate completion attempt and the return-to-dashboard state. The sample frame provides the wording and hierarchy to inspect; it does not establish that a delivery or payment occurred.

Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
A clear completion message closes the operational task without making unsupported payment promises.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

The handoff combines customer parcel entry with driver stop progress and completion states. Routing, delivery estimates, payments and updates across roles remain integration requirements. The screenshots describe the prototype sequence and its stated limits.
