Legacy design case study
Legacy customer prototype
Legacy driver prototype
WHERE THE WORK LANDED

The customer and driver views give the delivery lifecycle different priorities. Parcel entry, the next stop and the completion boundary can now be inspected in the case itself. A working routing or dispatch service, and any improvement in delivery performance, require evidence beyond these designs.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Compare the customer milestone with the driver action for pickup, arrival and completion; each pair should describe the same service event.
Walk through an intermediate-stop failure and delayed completion update. Check that the next action remains clear without implying settlement has occurred.
Looking back

The most consequential design work sits between the roles. A customer-facing milestone and a driver action must describe the same event, while delivery completion and financial settlement remain separate. The prototype makes those distinctions visible; a service review must still exercise delayed, failed and duplicate events.

text:
PERSONAL TOOLING · COMBAT-LOG INFORMATION DESIGN

NEVERWINTER LIVE PARSER
NEVERWINTER LIVE PARSER

Turning an event stream into an inspectable summary without making clean numbers look more certain than the underlying data.

CONTRIBUTION
Product design and frontend tooling
EVIDENCE
Public source files and implementation documentation

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN A COMBAT SUMMARY MAKE COMPLEX EVENTS READABLE WITHOUT HIDING THE ASSUMPTIONS BEHIND ITS NUMBERS?

The useful journey is from an encounter overview to the events behind a question. My information-design and frontend work focuses on keeping that connection inspectable, then making incomplete input distinguishable from a real zero. Code and calculation fixtures are the relevant artifacts for this personal tool.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Establish the encounter context
Move from overview to diagnosis
Expose uncertainty in the input
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

A combat parser sits between raw events and a player's explanation of an encounter. The interface needs to group and summarize information while retaining enough context to judge what a number represents. A polished total is not useful if the player cannot tell which encounter, actor, filter or time range produced it.

The public implementation is a Windows-oriented Electron application with a React renderer. Its repository separates parsing, encounter aggregation and renderer view-model tests. My portfolio scope concerns the information model, summary hierarchy and implementation-aware tooling; this is a personal project, separate from ownership of Neverwinter or its game data.

Constraints that shaped the work
A summary depends on grouping and calculation assumptions that the interface must not conceal.
Missing or ambiguous events can limit what may safely be inferred.
High-density tables need useful defaults without preventing deeper inspection.
01 / ESTABLISH THE ENCOUNTER CONTEXT

A number first needs enough context to be interpreted.

KEEP THE SUMMARY ATTACHED TO ITS CONTEXT

Encounter scope changes the meaning of every number. The renderer view-model tests include a case where a player has 999 total damage across the available data but only 120 in the selected encounter. The expected row uses the selected encounter’s 120 and derives 12 DPS for its ten-second duration. These are fixture values, not player performance claims.

That example makes the interface requirement specific: the selected encounter is part of the metric, and the summary should not silently fall back to a broader total. The linked source is an inspectable contract; this portfolio review has not independently executed that repository’s tests.

TRADE-OFF
A compact summary helps orientation but cannot hide the encounter and filter boundaries that define it.

02 / MOVE FROM OVERVIEW TO DIAGNOSIS

With the context established, the overview should lead into a specific question.

SEPARATE OVERVIEW FROM DIAGNOSIS

The implementation keeps raw-line parsing, encounter aggregation and renderer row construction in separate source areas. This supports an important distinction: an event’s applied amount, the way events are grouped, and the row a person reads are related but different decisions.

The parser tests specifically distinguish applied damage or healing from base magnitude. The renderer tests then cover ownership grouping, including player-owned summons and companions. An overview must make its grouping understandable so a clean total does not imply a different calculation.

TRADE-OFF
Progressive detail reduces noise while a clear route to events preserves inspectability.

03 / EXPOSE UNCERTAINTY IN THE INPUT

That investigation must also reveal when the source data cannot support an answer.

SHOW UNCERTAINTY AS A STATE OF THE DATA

The parser test suite contains an explicit malformed-line case. It expects an issue result and an unknown event type, rather than silently treating the input as valid combat damage. The renderer tests also distinguish zeroed placeholder encounters from encounters with meaningful combat totals.

These source cases give the uncertainty discussion something concrete to point to. They do not prove complete parser accuracy or the way every issue is announced in the UI; that requires execution and inspection of the application with representative logs.

Malformed-input contract from the actual parser test, excerpt
expect(result.kind).toBe("issue");
if (result.kind === "issue") {
  expect(result.issue.reason).toMatch(/separator|field count/i);
  expect(result.event.eventType).toBe("unknown");
}

Read the original source

TRADE-OFF
Visible uncertainty is less tidy than a zero, but avoids turning missing input into a false conclusion.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

The public source provides the strongest evidence here: parser cases, encounter aggregation and renderer view-model fixtures can be inspected separately. This review read those contracts and the application manifest; it did not run the Windows application or independently establish calculation accuracy.

Inspect real parser cases and malformed-input expectations
Inspect encounter aggregation fixture
Inspect encounter-scoped rows and ownership grouping
Read the Electron application and runtime manifest
WHERE THE WORK LANDED

An encounter summary is useful when its actor, time range and supporting events remain inspectable. Known fixtures are the right way to check those relationships and calculation limits. The portfolio account does not substitute a clean dashboard for parser-accuracy evidence.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Trace one displayed metric back to known combat events and the documented calculation rule.
Use empty, malformed and interrupted log fixtures before evaluating parsing correctness, session recovery or speed.
Looking back

A clean dashboard is only persuasive when its numbers can be traced back to the relevant events and calculation rules. I would prioritize that traceability over adding another headline statistic. Known input fixtures are required before reporting accuracy or performance improvements.

text:
ENTERPRISE SAAS · CRM AND SHARED WORKSPACE PATTERNS

ORKEST HQ
ORKEST HQ

A shared interface language for business software, with CRM screens that make ownership, qualification and the next action easier to inspect.

CONTRIBUTION
UX architecture and product design
EVIDENCE
Complete original Figma screens · sample design content

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN ONE WORKSPACE SUPPORT DIFFERENT BUSINESS JOBS WITHOUT MAKING PEOPLE RELEARN THE INTERFACE AT EVERY MODULE?

The CRM story starts before a form is opened: someone needs to recognize which leads require their attention. From there, capture should establish a usable record, and conversion should carry its history forward. I used that path to connect navigation, table hierarchy and action design instead of treating them as separate screens.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Find the work
Capture a usable lead
Carry context into conversion
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

Orkest brings CRM, sales, inventory and finance into a modular workspace. My challenge was to give that breadth a coherent structure without making every module behave like the same administrative table. A lead, an invoice and a stock movement can share navigation conventions while asking very different questions of the person using them.

My contribution covered the workspace architecture, navigation levels, record and table patterns, action hierarchy and information density. This case uses the current-labeled CRM frames in the supplied primary design file as its visual evidence. Other modules and draft states are part of the broader design context; they are not presented here as completed production features.

Constraints that shaped the work
Shared navigation must help people move between modules without erasing the task context.
Dense record lists need enough structure for comparison, while creation and review need a clearer action hierarchy.
A visible filter, view or button does not establish its implemented behavior or authorization rules.
01 / FIND THE WORK

First, the list has to explain whose work is visible.

SEPARATE OWNERSHIP FROM RECORD QUALIFICATION

The module directory establishes the broader workspace before the CRM list narrows the task. It groups business areas without requiring the person to remember where every capability lives. Entering CRM should preserve that sense of location while giving lead ownership and qualification their own hierarchy.

The leads design places All leads, My leads and Unassigned near search and Filters. These views describe ownership; qualification is represented inside the record list. Keeping those concepts separate gives a reviewer two useful questions: whose work is this, and what state is it in?

That separation also sets a handoff requirement. Switching an ownership view should have an explicit rule for existing filters, selection and the result count. The screenshot establishes the hierarchy, while the behavior still needs an agreed contract.

The complete filter sequence adds the next part of that list story: choose criteria, review a problem and inspect the resulting confirmation. These supporting form states are shown as designed scenarios alongside the current-labeled CRM core, not as proof of server behavior.

02 / CAPTURE A USABLE LEAD

Once a lead needs to be added, the interface changes from comparison to careful entry.

MAKE DEPENDENCIES VISIBLE BEFORE SAVING

The create-lead design groups contact information and qualification instead of scattering both across an undifferentiated form. Its side panel explains the capture-to-conversion sequence and says that the score is calculated after saving. That is a useful boundary: the interface should not imply that an unsaved value is already a reliable qualification result.

The remaining design-to-engineering questions are concrete: what may a draft omit, when is duplicate checking performed, who may assign an owner, and which values survive a failed save? Those questions belong beside this form rather than in a separate generic handoff document.

Editing is a different commitment from first capture. The edit form retains the record fields but adds explicit save behavior and duplicate-check guidance. That gives the handoff a concrete continuity rule: distinguish new input from an existing record and make the consequence of saving understandable.

TRADE-OFF
Grouping reduces visual competition; it also makes the required-versus-draft distinction more important.

03 / CARRY CONTEXT INTO CONVERSION

Saving is an intermediate step. The next design problem is moving the record forward without losing its context.

REUSE GRAMMAR WHERE THE OPERATIONAL JOB REPEATS

The shared system is a set of rules for location, records, status and action priority. It should reduce relearning when someone moves from a list into a detail view. It should also permit an exception when a module needs a different sequence or a more consequential review step.

I would judge reuse by whether the next task remains understandable, not by counting identical cards. For CRM, that means keeping the record identity and owner legible while allowing qualification and conversion to receive their own treatment.

The current lead-detail panel makes conversion readiness explicit: core information is complete, and conversion should preserve history while creating a contact and opportunity. That visible promise gives engineering a concrete consistency rule to implement and test.

Orkest full lead-detail workspace connects record identity, activity history and conversion readiness. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

TRADE-OFF
Shared components help orientation, while conversion needs its own consequential action and data rules.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

The useful handoff unit is a record workflow: entry conditions, data requirements, state changes and recovery, supported by reusable interface patterns. The reviewed exports show the visible design; they do not verify server validation, access control or synchronization between modules.

Inspect public repository
WHERE THE WORK LANDED

Ownership views, qualification and conversion are the central CRM decisions in this case. The current screens make those relationships inspectable. A useful task review would follow an unassigned lead through capture and conversion, including a failed save; no task-time or adoption measurement is available.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Find an unassigned lead, apply a filter and switch ownership views. Can the person explain which records are now included?
Follow a failed save into retry and conversion. Check that ownership, input and record history survive each transition.
Looking back

The important consistency is continuity of work. Reusing a table is useful only if ownership, qualification and the next action keep their meaning as a record moves forward. I would extend the shared grammar module by module, with explicit exceptions where the business object changes.

text:
TECHNICAL PLATFORM · WEBSITE DESIGN AND FRONTEND

SPLASHNODE
SPLASHNODE

Explaining content, device and data-management capabilities through a website whose design and implementation can inform each other.

CONTRIBUTION
Website designer and frontend contributor
EVIDENCE
Existing portfolio material; original screen evidence incomplete

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN A TECHNICAL PLATFORM WEBSITE HELP A BUYER CONNECT CAPABILITIES TO A REAL USE CASE?

The design path moves from recognizing a task to understanding a capability and choosing a way to evaluate it. Because my contribution includes frontend work, that path also has to survive real text and browser behavior. The website is the scope of this case, separate from the underlying platform.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Recognize a use case
Find the evaluation path
Test the composition in code
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

The existing project material describes Splashnode as a technical platform with content, device and data-management capabilities. The website's job is to help a prospective buyer understand where that platform fits before asking them to compare a long list of features.

My contribution spans website composition, capability explanation, responsive behavior and frontend implementation. This case concerns that website experience. It does not establish ownership of the underlying platform software or provide a verified commercial result.

Constraints that shaped the work
Technical capability needs enough explanation to be meaningful to a buyer.
Use cases and feature detail must support each other without repeating the same claim.
Implementation decisions need to preserve hierarchy under real content and viewport constraints.
01 / RECOGNIZE A USE CASE

Begin with the buyer’s task rather than a wall of feature names.

TRANSLATE A CAPABILITY INTO A RECOGNIZABLE TASK

A feature name is only useful when the visitor can connect it to something they need to accomplish. I organize the story around the problem or use case first, then explain the capability that supports it.

That order helps distinguish an introductory promise from the detail needed for evaluation. It also sets an editorial check: if a paragraph could describe any technical platform, it needs a more specific task or a narrower claim.

TRADE-OFF
Use cases make features meaningful; specific mechanism detail prevents the story becoming generic.

02 / FIND THE EVALUATION PATH

Once the capability is relevant, the visitor needs a way to investigate further.

KEEP THE ROUTE TO EVALUATION VISIBLE

The page should help a visitor decide whether to inspect more detail, view an example or make contact. Repeating the same high-pressure action after every section can interrupt that evaluation instead of supporting it.

I treat action placement as part of the information sequence. A call to action should follow enough context for the visitor to understand what the next step offers, without hiding that route until the end of a long page.

TRADE-OFF
Repeated calls to action improve availability but can interrupt evaluation when placed before enough context.

03 / TEST THE COMPOSITION IN CODE

The reading sequence then has to work outside the ideal desktop artboard.

LET THE BROWSER CHALLENGE THE COMPOSITION

Because my contribution includes frontend work, a layout can be reviewed with actual copy lengths, wrapping and navigation behavior. That feedback is useful while decisions are still easy to change.

The existing public preview is retained as evidence of the work's visual context. The implementation is part of the design discussion, rather than a separate downstream deliverable.

TRADE-OFF
Reusable sections support implementation while real content may require a deliberate exception.

EXISTING PORTFOLIO PREVIEW
Open image ↗

Retained portfolio presentation. A matching original Figma screen has not been verified for this case.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

The scope joins website UX with implementation-aware composition. Responsive layout, section hierarchy and reusable frontend patterns are part of the same deliverable. Backend platform capability and operational reliability remain outside the evidence shown by this case.

Public material for this case is limited. This account stays focused on my contribution, its design decisions and the questions that deserve further validation.

WHERE THE WORK LANDED

Design and frontend work meet in the browser: headings wrap, capability sections compete for attention and the route to evaluation has to remain visible. Those are inspectable delivery questions. Usage of the underlying platform and commercial outcomes are outside this website case.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask a buyer to connect one platform capability to a task in their own work, then find an appropriate evaluation step.
Review the page with real copy lengths and narrow viewports; check that the use-case explanation still leads naturally into capability detail.
Looking back

A technical website becomes useful when a visitor can connect the offer to their own job and identify a next step with enough context. Frontend work is valuable here because actual content challenges the composition before it becomes a fixed visual specification.

text:
HOSTING AND INFRASTRUCTURE · STATIC WEBSITE

GRID LABS
GRID LABS

A hosting offer organized around service fit, plan comparison and a clear route to the next commercial step.

CONTRIBUTION
Website and frontend design contribution
EVIDENCE
Owner-supplied website capture and original portfolio artwork

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN A HOSTING BUYER COMPARE PLANS WITHOUT CARRYING EVERY SPECIFICATION IN MEMORY?

The journey is a comparison problem before it is a purchase problem. My website contribution organizes the plan differences, considers what happens when cards stack on mobile, and makes the static frontend’s commercial boundary explicit.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Locate the meaningful difference
Compare on a narrow screen
Understand the next commercial step
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

Grid Labs is a hosting and infrastructure website in the existing portfolio. A prospective buyer needs to understand which service fits, how plans differ and what information is still required before choosing. Specifications matter, but a specification wall does not provide that sequence by itself.

My contribution covers commercial hierarchy, plan presentation, domain-search affordance, responsive layout and static frontend structure. The case is deliberately scoped to the website. A visible search field does not establish a functioning domain lookup, and a plan card does not prove provisioning or billing capability.

Constraints that shaped the work
Equivalent plan information needs a consistent order and unit.
Narrow screens make side-by-side comparison difficult.
The interface must remain honest about the difference between a static website and an operating service.
01 / LOCATE THE MEANINGFUL DIFFERENCE

Start by making equivalent plan attributes genuinely comparable.

MAKE PLAN DIFFERENCES EASY TO LOCATE

I start with the attributes that change the decision between plans. Those should remain in a stable order so the visitor can compare rather than remember a previous card. Supporting technical detail can remain available without giving every specification equal emphasis.

The review needs realistic prices, units and billing periods. Where current commercial terms are not verified, the portfolio should discuss the comparison pattern instead of repeating potentially outdated offers.

TRADE-OFF
A compact plan card supports scanning, while secondary specifications still need a reachable home.

02 / COMPARE ON A NARROW SCREEN

That structure faces its hardest test when the plans no longer fit side by side.

TREAT MOBILE COMPARISON AS AN INFORMATION PROBLEM

Stacking plan cards preserves content but weakens direct comparison. A useful narrow layout needs stable headings, repeated attribute labels and a clear association between price, period and included capability.

I would test a person comparing two plans with one meaningful difference. If the answer depends on remembering an offscreen card, the layout needs a stronger comparison aid or a more concise set of decision attributes.

TRADE-OFF
Stacked cards preserve content but weaken direct comparison; repeated labels help maintain context.

03 / UNDERSTAND THE NEXT COMMERCIAL STEP

Choosing a plan then leads beyond the limits of the static website.

KEEP SCOPE VISIBLE AT THE BOUNDARY OF THE SITE

A domain-search affordance can communicate a next step, but it must not imply a service the static implementation does not provide. Its actual destination and response behavior belong in the build review.

The same discipline applies to purchase calls to action. The website should establish what the visitor is continuing toward without inventing a complete account, checkout or hosting-management platform in the case study.

TRADE-OFF
A clear commercial affordance must describe its real destination rather than imply an unbuilt service.

FROM HOSTING OFFER TO LIVE PAGE

Explore the Grid Labs hosting website

WHERE THE WORK LANDED

Plan comparison depends on stable attributes, units and billing periods. The static website scope also limits what a domain-search or purchase affordance can promise. The case centers on those design and implementation boundaries, with current commercial terms left to the service owner.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask a buyer to choose between adjacent plans and explain which specification drove that choice.
Repeat the comparison on a narrow screen with longer plan labels; preserve units and distinctions without requiring horizontal page scrolling.
Looking back

The comparison pattern should reduce the amount of information a buyer has to remember. Stable labels and units are more useful than decorative emphasis on every plan. Provisioning, billing and current offer accuracy remain service-owner responsibilities.

text:
WORDPRESS AND ELEMENTOR · FURNITURE STARTER SITE

ZAKRA FURNITURE
ZAKRA FURNITURE

An image-led catalogue designed to remain coherent when real content replaces the demo.

CONTRIBUTION
Storefront UI and template design contribution
EVIDENCE
Existing portfolio material; original screen evidence incomplete

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN A FURNITURE STARTER SITE REMAIN COHERENT AFTER A SITE OWNER REPLACES THE DEMO CONTENT?

The polished demo is only the starting condition. My template design contribution considers what happens next: mixed photography enters the catalogue, product names wrap, and the site owner changes sections. This case follows those pressures from image treatment to the editing system.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Accommodate varied photography
Keep product details predictable
Let the owner change the catalogue
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

A furniture starter site has two users: the shopper browsing products and the site owner changing the catalogue. The initial composition needs to support both. An attractive demo that depends on identical image crops and short product names is a fragile template.

My existing contribution covers catalogue hierarchy, reusable storefront sections, product-card structure, typography, spacing and CMS-aware choices for WordPress and Elementor. This case does not establish ownership of the whole Zakra platform, a working inventory service or a completed ecommerce backend.

Constraints that shaped the work
Furniture photography varies in crop, visual weight and aspect ratio.
Product names, category sizes and section counts change after the template is delivered.
Site owners need editing freedom without having to redesign the page for every update.
01 / ACCOMMODATE VARIED PHOTOGRAPHY

The first source of variation is the photography itself.

GIVE PHOTOGRAPHY A PREDICTABLE FRAME

The catalogue needs a repeatable image treatment so a mix of product photographs still reads as one system. The choice is a trade-off: a fixed crop can improve rhythm but remove part of a product, while an uncropped image can create uneven whitespace.

I would review both approaches with varied source images and decide according to the product category. The rule should be explicit rather than dependent on manually preparing every demo asset.

TRADE-OFF
Fixed crops create rhythm but can remove product detail; uncropped images preserve detail with less uniform whitespace.

02 / KEEP PRODUCT DETAILS PREDICTABLE

A stable image treatment still leaves the rest of the product card to handle change.

KEEP THE PRODUCT-CARD CONTRACT STABLE

Names, category cues and decision details need predictable placement. A shopper should not have to relearn a card because a product name wraps onto another line or an optional field is absent.

For a template, that means reviewing long names, missing images, different product counts and narrow layouts. Those cases are part of the design brief for reusable content, not exceptions to be hidden from the portfolio.

TRADE-OFF
A stable card hierarchy supports scanning without assuming every product has identical content.

03 / LET THE OWNER CHANGE THE CATALOGUE

Those repeated cards belong to sections a site owner needs to edit over time.

MAKE EDITABILITY PART OF THE UX

A site owner needs to understand which sections can be repeated, removed or rearranged. Simple spacing and typography rules give the editor useful freedom while limiting accidental visual drift.

The work is therefore more than a single storefront screenshot. Its value lies in the rules that help a catalogue survive ordinary editing. Those rules need to be evaluated with varied catalogue content, rather than judged only against the demo composition.

TRADE-OFF
Editing freedom helps the owner; a small set of spacing and type rules limits accidental drift.

EXISTING PORTFOLIO PREVIEW
Open image ↗

Retained portfolio presentation. A matching original Figma screen has not been verified for this case.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

The scope is a reusable starter-site interface and its content behavior. Existing public material is retained. The design discussion stays distinct from claims about checkout, stock accuracy, order fulfillment or sales performance.

View Zakra Furniture starter-site preview
WHERE THE WORK LANDED

A reusable storefront has to survive ordinary catalogue editing. Varied image crops, longer names and missing optional content are practical tests for the card and section rules described here. A polished demo alone cannot establish checkout or sales performance.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Replace demo content with long product names, inconsistent photograph proportions and missing descriptions; check that the catalogue hierarchy survives.
Ask a site owner to edit a category and product card, then inspect the result on a narrow screen without manually repairing the layout.
Looking back

A template is a set of decisions that someone else keeps using. Its quality becomes clearer under ordinary content variation than under a perfectly art-directed demo. The next review needs varied catalogue fixtures; checkout behavior and sales performance are outside this design account.

text:
LUXURY FASHION RENTAL MARKETPLACE

DESIGNEREX
DESIGNEREX

Balancing image-led fashion discovery with the stable rental information needed to compare listings.

CONTRIBUTION
Design contribution within a broader marketplace
EVIDENCE
Existing portfolio material; original screen evidence incomplete

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

HOW CAN FASHION DISCOVERY STAY EXPRESSIVE WHILE MAKING RENTAL DECISIONS DEPENDABLE?

A rental browse journey moves from attraction to comparison. My contribution focuses on that shift: let photography introduce the garment, give recurring details a stable place, and preserve the browsing context as a person explores. The case stays within that contribution to the wider marketplace.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Notice the garment
Compare practical details
Continue without losing context
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

Designerex is presented in my existing portfolio as a luxury fashion rental marketplace. The interface has to support interest in a garment and practical evaluation of a rental. Photography can establish desire, but it cannot answer questions about size, availability or terms on its own.

My contribution is limited to browsing and listing patterns, visual hierarchy and the relationship between images and decision details. This case does not claim end-to-end ownership of the marketplace or a measured change in bookings. The account is limited to my part of the browsing and listing experience.

Constraints that shaped the work
Large photography needs to coexist with readable listing information.
A comparison grid becomes harder to use when equivalent attributes change position or format.
A team contribution must remain distinct from ownership of the whole product.
01 / NOTICE THE GARMENT

The first job of the listing is to invite a closer look.

GIVE THE PHOTOGRAPH AND THE METADATA DIFFERENT JOBS

The photograph is the entry point to the item. The repeated listing structure is what lets someone evaluate several items without reconstructing the information every time. I approach the card as a relationship between both, rather than choosing between a purely editorial tile and a specification-heavy product block.

The design trade-off is density. Adding every rental condition to a grid can obscure the garments, while removing every practical attribute pushes too much work into detail pages.

TRADE-OFF
Image prominence creates interest, but essential rental attributes must remain visible.

02 / COMPARE PRACTICAL DETAILS

Interest is not enough to choose a rental; comparable details become the priority.

KEEP COMPARABLE INFORMATION IN COMPARABLE PLACES

Stable labels and placement make the repeated pattern useful. A person should not have to inspect a different part of each card to find an equivalent rental attribute. The detail page can then carry the depth that would overfill the browse view.

A practical review would compare several listings with different image crops, long names and unavailable options. That is a proposed evaluation, not a claim that the current marketplace has passed it.

TRADE-OFF
Stable card metadata supports comparison; detailed terms belong at a deeper level.

03 / CONTINUE WITHOUT LOSING CONTEXT

As the person moves into detail and back, interaction must protect the work they have already done.

KEEP PREMIUM PRESENTATION OUT OF THE WAY OF THE TASK

Visual restraint helps the product remain the focus. Navigation, filtering and actions should support the catalogue instead of demanding their own performance. A quieter interaction convention can still express the brand through typography, spacing and image treatment.

I would inspect keyboard access, filter feedback and returning from a detail page alongside visual craft. A premium browse experience still needs a predictable route back to the person's previous context.

TRADE-OFF
Quiet controls support the catalogue while still needing clear focus and active-filter feedback.

EXISTING PORTFOLIO PREVIEW
Open image ↗

Retained portfolio presentation. A matching original Figma screen has not been verified for this case.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

This is a scoped account of marketplace UI contribution. Existing public references are preserved. The public account stays within the contribution and artifacts I can describe without claiming ownership of the whole marketplace.

Public material for this case is limited. This account stays focused on my contribution, its design decisions and the questions that deserve further validation.

WHERE THE WORK LANDED

The design tension is between image-led browsing and dependable rental comparison. The card and detail hierarchy should be reviewed with varied garment photos, long names and unavailable options. That is the contribution described here, within the broader marketplace team.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask a renter to compare two garments for occasion, size, price and availability without relying on memory.
Review a long garment name, an unavailable date and a missing photograph to check whether the rental decision remains understandable.
Looking back

Premium presentation earns its place when it helps someone judge a garment without hiding the rental decision. Photography creates interest; stable metadata lets a renter turn that interest into a dependable comparison.

text:
ARCHIVED FRONTEND LEARNING · SASS AND BUILD WORKFLOW

SASSBOILERPLATE
SASSBOILERPLATE

A learning archive that traces a small Sass structure through an existing Gulp-based build, with its upstream origin kept explicit.

CONTRIBUTION
Frontend learning and starter-workflow adaptation
EVIDENCE
Public source files and implementation documentation

THE PRODUCT QUESTION

WHAT DID A SMALL STARTER WORKFLOW TEACH ME ABOUT MAKING FRONTEND STRUCTURE UNDERSTANDABLE?

This case is a deliberately modest learning story. Start at the Sass entry, follow the shared import into base rules, then look at how the build transforms the files. The archive makes that path inspectable without turning a borrowed starter into a claim of original framework authorship.

FOLLOW THE DESIGN PATH

Follow the Sass entry
Inspect the build responsibilities
Keep the archive in its proper scope
CONTEXT AND MY CONTRIBUTION

SassBoilerplate is an earlier frontend learning archive, not an independently authored framework. The archived README identifies it as a historical copy of JR Cologne’s Gulp Starter Kit, with Sass, Pug, Babel, BrowserSync and image-processing tasks. That provenance is part of the project, not a detail to omit from the portfolio.

The useful story is what the files make inspectable: an entry point, a small shared import layer and build tasks that turn authored assets into output. My contribution is presented as learning and adaptation around that workflow, rather than ownership of the upstream kit or a maintained npm package.

Constraints that shaped the work
Attribute the original JR Cologne starter kit and preserve its distinction from this learning archive.
Describe the source that exists: the current shared Sass import points to the base rules; empty architecture placeholders were removed.
Historical tooling and dependencies are not a verified recommendation for a new production project.
01 / FOLLOW THE SASS ENTRY

The entry point gives the first concrete place to inspect the workflow.

START WITH THE FILES THAT ACTUALLY CONTRIBUTE STYLES

The archived app.sass imports _includes; _includes imports base/_base. That is a small, visible dependency path. The source comments explicitly say that empty helper, module, partial and global placeholders were removed, so the case should not describe a large token or component architecture that is no longer there.

The design principle is legibility: a file’s name and import should explain its responsibility. For this archive, the honest example is a short chain a reader can inspect directly.

Actual entry and shared import, excerpted from the learning archive
// app.sass
@import '_includes'

// _includes.sass
@import 'base/_base'

Read the original source

TRADE-OFF
A small import layer is easy to follow; adding categories before they own real styles creates structure without a useful responsibility.

02 / INSPECT THE BUILD RESPONSIBILITIES

After locating the Sass source, the next question is how it becomes browser output.

READ THE BUILD AS A SEQUENCE OF RESPONSIBILITIES

The archived sassTask reads Sass and SCSS, initializes source maps, handles errors, resolves dependents, compiles, prefixes and minifies CSS, writes maps and sends the result to the output directory and BrowserSync. Separate named tasks handle templates, JavaScript, images and copied dependencies.

Those boundaries make the workflow easier to explain than a list of tools alone. They also expose where a modern migration needs care: an old compiler or image dependency can fail even when the Sass source itself is simple.

TRADE-OFF
Automation removes repetitive work, while every additional transform introduces another compatibility and debugging boundary.

03 / KEEP THE ARCHIVE IN ITS PROPER SCOPE

The last decision is how to present and reuse the work responsibly.

TREAT THE ARCHIVE AS EVIDENCE OF LEARNING

The archived README names the upstream package, original author, repository and MIT license. It also warns that the historical Node requirement and dependencies do not establish compatibility with a current runtime. That is the appropriate boundary for this portfolio entry.

The artifact is useful for explaining how I learned to connect source organization and build behavior. It is not a new framework release, a currently maintained package, or evidence of measured developer onboarding gains.

TRADE-OFF
Keeping historical work shows the learning path, provided its attribution and present-day limits remain clear.

ARTIFACTS AND DELIVERY BOUNDARY

A public learning archive with inspectable Sass imports and named Gulp build tasks. The original starter kit is credited to JR Cologne. This review inspected the source and documentation; it did not install or execute the historical dependency tree.

Read the archive status and upstream attribution
Inspect the actual named build tasks
Follow the Sass entry point
WHERE THE WORK LANDED

The archive supports a concrete explanation of source ownership, import direction and build responsibilities. Its value in the portfolio is the learning and adaptation, with upstream attribution and maintenance limits visible.

How I would evaluate the design

These are proposed review tasks, not reported research findings.

Ask a developer unfamiliar with the archive to locate the source styles, build entry point and generated output.
Review upstream attribution and dependency age before deciding what can be learned from the structure or reused in a maintained project.
Looking back

The useful lesson is to make responsibility and provenance easy to follow. A starter can support learning without needing to become a product claim. Today I would review a small maintained toolchain against the actual project rather than recommend this historical dependency set unchanged.

PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

RESPONSIVE SAAS DASHBOARD HANDOFF NOTES THAT ENGINEERS CAN USE
RESPONSIVE SAAS DASHBOARD HANDOFF NOTES THAT ENGINEERS CAN USE

A responsive dashboard needs rules for priority, overflow and continuation. A desktop frame and a mobile frame leave the hardest decisions between them.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-07-08
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Write the task that must survive
Specify behavior by constraint
Use the desktop evidence honestly
Document overflow and interruption
Test the transition, not only the endpoints
WRITE THE TASK THAT MUST SURVIVE

Start with a concrete task such as locating an unassigned lead and inspecting its status. That gives the responsive design a priority. A small screen may not need every desktop column, but it still needs record identity, current state and a usable route to the next action.

Do not describe responsive behavior as simply hiding secondary information. Name what is secondary for this task, where it remains available and what the person can no longer do in the condensed view.

SPECIFY BEHAVIOR BY CONSTRAINT
Specify behavior by constraint
Element	Rule to document	Review condition
Navigation	When and how it condenses	Location and current module remain understandable
Table	Column priority and overflow behavior	A record can still be identified
Filters	Panel entry, applied state and dismissal	The result context remains visible
Actions	Which remain persistent	The primary task is reachable without overlap
Detail	Reading order and expandable groups	Labels stay associated with their values
USE THE DESKTOP EVIDENCE HONESTLY

The Orkest leads screen gives a concrete desktop hierarchy: ownership views, search, Filters and qualification states. It is useful for deciding which relationships to protect. It does not show a reviewed mobile filter panel or prove that all responsive states are implemented.

When mobile evidence is incomplete, write the proposed behavior as a requirement and test it in the build. Do not place an unrelated phone screenshot next to the article and call it responsive proof.

Orkest leads workspace with summary cards, ownership views, search, filters and the complete record table. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

DOCUMENT OVERFLOW AND INTERRUPTION

Decide whether wide data scrolls inside a labeled region, changes representation or moves into a detail view. If columns are removed, say how the person reaches them. Keep sort and selection behavior explicit when the representation changes.

Also inspect the mobile keyboard, fixed navigation, long translated labels and zoom. A layout that fits in a static screenshot can still hide the save action when the keyboard opens or leave focus behind a fixed control.

TEST THE TRANSITION, NOT ONLY THE ENDPOINTS

Resize with a selected row, an open panel and active filters. Check what persists and where focus goes. Review intermediate widths where neither the ideal desktop nor ideal mobile composition fits comfortably.

A useful acceptance note names an observable result: the record identifier remains visible; the selected action is reachable; the page itself does not overflow; closing a panel returns focus sensibly. Those checks are more durable than one breakpoint number copied from an artboard.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

SAAS DASHBOARD FILTER UX FOR REAL OPERATIONAL WORK
SAAS DASHBOARD FILTER UX FOR REAL OPERATIONAL WORK

A filter changes the answer a table gives. People need to see the question currently being asked, understand why a record is absent and change that question without losing context.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-07-03
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Separate a recurring view from a temporary condition
Make the current query inspectable
Decide persistence before building the panel
Make zero results recoverable
Review with an operational question
SEPARATE A RECURRING VIEW FROM A TEMPORARY CONDITION

A recurring view answers a familiar question such as which leads belong to me. A filter narrows that view with conditions such as status or date. A saved view may combine both, but the distinction should still be understandable.

The Orkest design separates All leads, My leads and Unassigned from search and Filters. That is visible evidence of the hierarchy, not proof of the open panel's behavior. The design review still needs to decide how conditions combine and persist.

Orkest leads workspace with summary cards, ownership views, search, filters and the complete record table. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

MAKE THE CURRENT QUERY INSPECTABLE

After applying conditions, show enough information to explain the result. A generic Filters badge with a count may be sufficient for a small panel, but a complex query often needs readable conditions. Define whether status is A or B and whether that group is combined with another condition using AND.

Avoid making a person reopen the panel just to explain why a record is missing. A compact summary should be understandable without exposing the entire query builder at all times.

DECIDE PERSISTENCE BEFORE BUILDING THE PANEL
Decide persistence before building the panel
Transition	Question to resolve
Switch ownership view	Are compatible conditions retained, reset or explicitly changed?
Open a record and return	Are filters, sort, page and scroll restored?
Refresh or share a URL	Which query state is encoded and safe to share?
Remove one condition	Does focus remain in a predictable place?
Clear all	Does it also clear search and the selected view?
MAKE ZERO RESULTS RECOVERABLE

An empty filtered table should retain the conditions that explain it. Use language such as No leads match these filters when that is the known cause, then offer a relevant change. Do not replace the query with a blank onboarding state that suggests no data exists.

Keep a useful result count and check how its update is communicated. For implementations that update without moving focus, W3C's status-message guidance helps distinguish a result announcement from an unnecessary focus change.

W3C guidance on status messages
REVIEW WITH AN OPERATIONAL QUESTION

Ask someone to find their unassigned work, add a condition, inspect a record and return. Then create a zero-result query and ask them to explain the absence. Observe where the interface forces them to remember hidden state.

The success condition is not that the panel opens. It is that the person understands the active query and can revise it. Keep performance and access restrictions in the review too: a slow result and a restricted result need different explanations.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

ROLE-BASED SAAS DASHBOARD UX WITHOUT DUPLICATING THE PRODUCT
ROLE-BASED SAAS DASHBOARD UX WITHOUT DUPLICATING THE PRODUCT

Role-based UX is not a reason to duplicate every screen. Share the meaning of a record and its states, then change the information and actions according to the job.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-07-02
Updated 4 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Distinguish three different concepts
Map tasks and actions before designing variants
Share the language, vary the priority
Design denial without leaking information
Test the boundary outside the happy path
Judge the model by a shared scenario
Inspect the denied state as a design artifact
DISTINGUISH THREE DIFFERENT CONCEPTS

A role describes a responsibility or access context. Ownership describes a relationship to a record. A view organizes a question someone regularly asks. Mixing those concepts produces interfaces where a label such as My leads appears to promise an authorization boundary that may not exist.

In the Orkest CRM design, All leads, My leads and Unassigned are visible views. They show an ownership model, not evidence that the backend enforces who can read or change a record.

Orkest leads workspace with summary cards, ownership views, search, filters and the complete record table. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

MAP TASKS AND ACTIONS BEFORE DESIGNING VARIANTS
Map tasks and actions before designing variants
Review dimension	Specify separately
Record visibility	Which records may this person read?
Field visibility	Which details may be disclosed?
Action	May they create, edit, assign, approve or export?
Transition	What state change can that action cause?
Recovery	What happens after access changes or an operation is denied?
SHARE THE LANGUAGE, VARY THE PRIORITY

piHub's creditor, investor and administrator journeys provide another useful design context. Different people inspect the same broader process for different reasons. A creditor may need outstanding requirements, while an administrator needs review context. Reusing the state vocabulary can help the product remain coherent without making both screens identical.

Those prototypes are separate design artifacts. They do not establish synchronized updates or real permission enforcement. A source-linked case study should keep that distinction visible rather than presenting visual role coverage as security verification.

DESIGN DENIAL WITHOUT LEAKING INFORMATION

An unavailable action needs an explanation appropriate to the situation. Hiding an action may simplify a routine view; showing a disabled action can explain a dependency. Neither choice by itself establishes security. The server must decide whether the request is allowed.

Be careful about revealing the existence of restricted records. Work with the product and engineering owners to decide what can safely be said, then make the recovery path useful within that boundary.

TEST THE BOUNDARY OUTSIDE THE HAPPY PATH
Open a direct record URL with a different role.
Attempt the same action after ownership or access changes.
Check export, search and bulk actions as well as individual buttons.
Return to a stale tab after a session or permission change.
Confirm that the interface explains the result without claiming a save that did not occur.
JUDGE THE MODEL BY A SHARED SCENARIO

Trace one example record across the relevant roles and write down what each person sees and may do. This makes inconsistencies easier to discuss than a gallery of disconnected dashboards. It also separates a design proposal from the engineering evidence required to call the permission model verified.

INSPECT THE DENIED STATE AS A DESIGN ARTIFACT

The piHub administrator page includes the denial design below. It gives the person a Go Back route, but the screenshot cannot answer whether a direct request is blocked correctly or whether the explanation discloses too much.

Use an authorized test account to check those questions in the implementation. Keep the visual state, the permission rule and server enforcement as separate evidence.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

SAAS DASHBOARD EMPTY STATES THAT HELP USERS RECOVER
SAAS DASHBOARD EMPTY STATES THAT HELP USERS RECOVER

An empty state is useful when someone can continue from it. Test the transition, retained input and result of the recovery action, not only the appearance of the panel.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-07-01
Updated 4 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Name what must remain intact
Test a transition matrix
Keep focus and announcements useful
Prevent recovery from becoming a repeated mistake
Record the result at task level
Review what a return action can recover
NAME WHAT MUST REMAIN INTACT

Before designing a recovery action, list the context the person may still need: search terms, active filters, selected workspace, sort order, page position and unsaved input. A recovery that silently resets all of it can create more work than the original empty result.

Separate recoverable context from stale or unsafe context. A selection from a previous permission scope may need to be cleared. The important point is to decide and explain the rule rather than letting it emerge accidentally from a rerender.

TEST A TRANSITION MATRIX
Test a transition matrix
Scenario	Recovery action	Acceptance question
No search matches	Edit or clear the query	Does the query remain available to revise?
Conflicting filters	Remove one condition	Can the person see which condition changed?
Loading failed	Retry	Is valid context retained and the request outcome explained?
Setup completed	Return to the module	Does the new state reflect the completed prerequisite?
Access changed	Reload or request access	Is restricted context handled consistently?
New data arrives	Refresh or observe an update	Does empty become loaded without a misleading intermediate result?
KEEP FOCUS AND ANNOUNCEMENTS USEFUL

A changed result does not always need a focus jump. Keep the person near the control they are using unless the next task genuinely requires moving them. If a brief status changes without receiving focus, make that information available to assistive technology in an appropriate way.

W3C's status-message guidance distinguishes those updates from a change of context. Use it to review the behavior, then test the actual implementation rather than assuming an accessibility attribute is sufficient.

W3C status-message guidance
PREVENT RECOVERY FROM BECOMING A REPEATED MISTAKE

A retry button needs a meaningful retry boundary. If the underlying prerequisite is still absent, repeating the same request may accomplish nothing. Explain the dependency or offer the action that can change it.

For record creation or other consequential operations, determine whether the first attempt may already have succeeded before offering another submission. The interface should not imply certainty when the request outcome is unknown.

RECORD THE RESULT AT TASK LEVEL

Write a short observation: the query was retained, the person removed one filter, the result returned and focus remained on the relevant control. That is stronger evidence than marking the empty-state component complete because its spacing matches the design.

This article covers recovery verification. Use the taxonomy article to classify causes and the concise guide to write the message that introduces the recovery.

REVIEW WHAT A RETURN ACTION CAN RECOVER

The piHub denial state offers Go Back. In an implementation review, test where that action leads after a direct deep link as well as after normal navigation. Browser history may not contain a useful permitted page.

That is a recovery requirement exposed by the design, not a reproduced defect in a live piHub service. The result belongs in the ledger only after the actual route and account conditions have been tested.

PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

DESIGN SYSTEMS FOR SMALL PRODUCT TEAMS WITHOUT OVERBUILDING
DESIGN SYSTEMS FOR SMALL PRODUCT TEAMS WITHOUT OVERBUILDING

A small team needs a reliable way to repeat and change decisions. It does not need to reproduce the operating model of a much larger organization.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-06-29
Updated 4 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Start where repetition already costs something
Give each shared pattern a small contract
Use real examples to limit variants
Document the escape hatch
Measure continuation rather than library size
Use a small product panel to test the boundary
START WHERE REPETITION ALREADY COSTS SOMETHING

Audit a few current screens and identify repeated decisions: field labels, validation, spacing, action hierarchy or table states. Choose a pattern that is used often enough to justify a shared contract. A hypothetical future component is a weaker starting point than a repeated inconsistency the team already maintains.

Keep the first scope small. A handful of semantic tokens and a well-specified form pattern can be more useful than a library with hundreds of incomplete variants.

GIVE EACH SHARED PATTERN A SMALL CONTRACT
Give each shared pattern a small contract
Part	Minimum useful explanation
Purpose	When to use it and what it is responsible for
Inputs	Required content and optional variation
States	Behavior under loading, error and unavailability
Constraints	Responsive and content limits
Ownership	Who reviews a change and where it is recorded
USE REAL EXAMPLES TO LIMIT VARIANTS

Before adding another variant, find the use case that requires it. If the difference is only temporary content, it may not need a new component shape. If it changes behavior or information priority, it deserves a more explicit review.

Keep product decisions outside the shared component when they are not genuinely reusable. A primary button should not know whether a specific financial application is eligible for approval. The product owns that rule.

DOCUMENT THE ESCAPE HATCH

An exception process can be a short note: what changed, why the shared pattern was insufficient and whether the result should be reused. This gives the team room to solve a real task without silently fragmenting the interface.

Review repeated exceptions periodically. They may reveal a missing capability, an unclear contract or a pattern that no longer fits. Deleting a weak abstraction can be a system improvement.

MEASURE CONTINUATION RATHER THAN LIBRARY SIZE

Ask another teammate to use and modify a pattern without a verbal tour. Inspect what they misunderstand and which questions the documentation fails to answer. Check a built usage with long content and an error state.

For a small team, the useful result is a shorter path from a product decision to a coherent implementation. Treat that as something to observe, not an efficiency percentage to invent because a component library exists.

USE A SMALL PRODUCT PANEL TO TEST THE BOUNDARY

Orkest combines a readiness message with a conversion action in the panel below. The panel can share text and action styling with other tasks, while the CRM owns the rule for readiness and the records that conversion creates.

That is a useful limit for a small library: reuse the presentation without embedding one product workflow in a generic component.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

A DESIGN HANDOFF CHECKLIST FOR STARTUP PRODUCT TEAMS
A DESIGN HANDOFF CHECKLIST FOR STARTUP PRODUCT TEAMS

A small team needs enough agreement to build safely, without turning every change into a specification project. Use this checklist for a release slice, not the entire product at once.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-06-28
Updated 4 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Define the slice and its boundary
Check readiness across four responsibilities
Run the minimum state review
Assign open questions before estimating completion
Review the implementation, then preserve the decision
Turn a visible promise into a release check
DEFINE THE SLICE AND ITS BOUNDARY

Name the user, starting point, task and endpoint. Creating a lead is a manageable slice; redesigning CRM is not. List what is deliberately outside the release so an attractive prototype does not quietly become a promise of unsupported behavior.

Attach one primary frame or flow as the current source. Keep older alternatives available if they explain a decision, but label them so engineering does not have to infer which version is approved.

CHECK READINESS ACROSS FOUR RESPONSIBILITIES
Check readiness across four responsibilities
Responsibility	Ready means	Evidence
Product	Rules and exceptions are decided	A short state or decision table
Design	Task, content and states are understandable	Reviewed frames and behavior notes
Engineering	Dependencies and failure boundaries are known	Integration assumptions and constraints
QA	Acceptance is observable	A short set of task-based checks
RUN THE MINIMUM STATE REVIEW
Start with realistic data, including a long label and a missing optional value.
Complete the main task and identify the saved result.
Trigger a correctable error and confirm that valid input is preserved.
Interrupt the operation and define what retry means.
Check an unavailable action or permission boundary.
Use a keyboard and a narrow viewport to reach the same endpoint.
ASSIGN OPEN QUESTIONS BEFORE ESTIMATING COMPLETION

A release checklist should make uncertainty visible. Give each open question an owner and explain which task it blocks. If the integration is unavailable, the team can still review layout and content, but it should not describe that review as end-to-end validation.

Keep conditional acceptance explicit. A flow may be visually ready while its authorization behavior is unverified. Recording both states is more useful than one green label for the entire feature.

REVIEW THE IMPLEMENTATION, THEN PRESERVE THE DECISION

Before release, repeat the agreed checks in the build. Record material differences, their consequence and the decision to repair or accept them. Do not make an acceptance test less demanding simply because the implementation took a different path.

Afterward, update the current artifact and retain a short change record. A startup does not need a large design-operations system to preserve why a consequential choice was made; it needs one reliable place where the next person can find it.

TURN A VISIBLE PROMISE INTO A RELEASE CHECK

The current Orkest lead-detail panel says conversion should preserve history and create a contact and opportunity. That gives a handoff checklist a concrete question: after conversion, can the reviewer trace the new records back to the lead and its activity?

The panel shows the intended rule. A release check still needs a valid record, a failed attempt and a repeated action so the team can verify what actually persists.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

HOW TO PRIORITIZE UX AUDIT FINDINGS BEFORE A REDESIGN
HOW TO PRIORITIZE UX AUDIT FINDINGS BEFORE A REDESIGN

A long issue list becomes useful when the team can explain why one problem deserves attention before another. Separate user consequence, evidence confidence and delivery effort.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-06-27
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Start with consequence, not the screenshot
Keep confidence visible
Use an order the team can defend
Separate quick repair from structural work
Keep a decision ledger
Revisit priority after learning
START WITH CONSEQUENCE, NOT THE SCREENSHOT

A visually obvious issue can be less consequential than a rare failure that loses work or prevents access. Describe what happens to the task: blocked, completed incorrectly, recoverable with extra work or merely less comfortable.

Keep severity separate from frequency. A single observed destructive failure may deserve immediate investigation even when its prevalence is unknown. Conversely, a frequently seen cosmetic difference does not automatically justify structural redesign.

KEEP CONFIDENCE VISIBLE
Keep confidence visible
Evidence state	Reasonable action
Reproduced failure	Repair or explicitly accept the known consequence
Observed once with clear conditions	Reproduce and investigate while preserving evidence
Consistent reported theme	Inspect the affected task and corroborate the cause
Expert concern	Frame as a hypothesis or targeted review
Preference	Treat as a design choice unless a consequence is established
USE AN ORDER THE TEAM CAN DEFEND

My preferred starting order is access and data integrity, blocked core tasks, repeated recovery costs, confusing decisions and then polish. The exact order depends on the product, but naming the reason makes it possible to challenge the decision constructively.

Do not multiply guessed values into a precise-looking score. If occurrence is unknown, write unknown. If delivery effort has not been assessed by engineering, keep it provisional. The discussion should reveal uncertainty rather than hide it inside arithmetic.

SEPARATE QUICK REPAIR FROM STRUCTURAL WORK

An incorrect label may be a small repair with a meaningful benefit. Several inconsistent states may indicate a shared component or data-model problem. Group related symptoms before estimating fixes so the team does not repeatedly patch the same cause.

Also record dependencies. A design repair can be ready while an API contract is unresolved. That does not make the whole item complete, and it should not prevent unrelated verified repairs from moving forward.

KEEP A DECISION LEDGER
Finding and affected task.
Observed consequence and evidence link.
Severity and confidence, recorded separately.
Proposed repair and accountable owner.
Dependency or decision that blocks progress.
Verification that will demonstrate the repair.
Reason for accepting or deferring the issue.
REVISIT PRIORITY AFTER LEARNING

Priority is a current decision, not a permanent property of a ticket. A reproduced failure, a changed release scope or new evidence can change the order. Keep the original observation and record why the decision changed.

A good audit creates a smaller set of consequential decisions and a reliable verification path. Closing a large number of low-value tickets is not a substitute for resolving the task failures that matter.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

WHEN A STARTUP NEEDS A UX AUDIT BEFORE A REDESIGN
WHEN A STARTUP NEEDS A UX AUDIT BEFORE A REDESIGN

A redesign is a commitment to change. An audit is useful when the team first needs to understand which change is warranted and which existing behavior should be preserved.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-06-26
Updated 4 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Identify the decision you cannot yet make
Choose a response that matches the evidence
Scope the audit around a consequential journey
Ask for a decision-ready deliverable
Do not delay urgent repairs for the perfect study
Bound a review around one driver decision
IDENTIFY THE DECISION YOU CANNOT YET MAKE

The interface looks old is not enough to choose a redesign scope. The useful uncertainty might be why onboarding stalls, whether navigation matches user tasks or whether a feature is hidden behind an access problem. Name that uncertainty before commissioning a broad visual refresh.

An audit is a good next step when the team has symptoms but cannot connect them to a defensible repair. If the defect is already known and reproducible, fixing it may be more useful than paying for another report.

CHOOSE A RESPONSE THAT MATCHES THE EVIDENCE
Choose a response that matches the evidence
Situation	Useful next move
A known broken save	Repair and regression-test the failure
Conflicting explanations for abandonment	Collect evidence around the affected task
A new role or business model	Review the task and information architecture
Inconsistent UI with stable behavior	Assess component and content-system repair
A new visual direction only	Bound the visual work and protect existing behavior
SCOPE THE AUDIT AROUND A CONSEQUENTIAL JOURNEY

For a small team, start with one important role and one end-to-end task. Include entry, input, waiting, failure and completion. Identify the integrations and account states needed to test it.

The Zapp parcel step is an example of a bounded review object. It can be inspected as part of a booking journey without pretending that a single screen explains dispatch, payment and delivery operations. A sensible scope makes those boundaries explicit.

ASK FOR A DECISION-READY DELIVERABLE

The output should contain reproducible findings, consequences, confidence, a proposed repair order and a verification plan. It should distinguish copy fixes, interaction changes, structural redesign and engineering defects.

Avoid a scope that promises a predetermined redesign regardless of what the evidence shows. An audit should be able to conclude that a smaller repair is enough, that more evidence is needed or that a part of the existing product deserves protection.

DO NOT DELAY URGENT REPAIRS FOR THE PERFECT STUDY

A clear access failure, data loss or broken critical path deserves attention while broader investigation continues. Record the original condition and test the repair. There is no need to wait for every secondary finding before addressing a verified problem.

For less certain concerns, make the next experiment small and reversible. The goal is a better product decision with a known basis, not a larger design programme justified by the existence of an audit.

BOUND A REVIEW AROUND ONE DRIVER DECISION

The Zapp driver design has a confirmed pickup, a named next drop-off, progress, an arrival action and an intermediate-stop issue route. That is enough to define a focused review: can the driver identify the current stop and explain the two actions?

The prototype says navigation is inactive. An audit scope should therefore separate task comprehension from real routing, live location and dispatch integration.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

HIRING A PRODUCT DESIGNER IN NEPAL FOR SAAS OR WEB3 WORK
HIRING A PRODUCT DESIGNER IN NEPAL FOR SAAS OR WEB3 WORK

Evaluate the work against your product's decisions, collaboration needs and evidence gaps. Location is one practical consideration; it should not substitute for examining the contribution.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Start with the kind of complexity you need help with
Inspect contribution, artifact and boundary together
Use a focused conversation
Check collaboration with a real problem
Choose the engagement that fits the uncertainty
START WITH THE KIND OF COMPLEXITY YOU NEED HELP WITH

A role description that asks for SaaS, fintech and Web3 experience can hide very different problems. Are you changing a multi-role workflow, building a component system, explaining a technical product or improving a mobile transaction journey? Name the task and the consequence before comparing portfolios.

For a Nepal-based remote designer, also agree the overlap hours, communication expectations and employment or contract arrangement. Confirm those details directly rather than assuming a country implies a particular availability or legal arrangement.

INSPECT CONTRIBUTION, ARTIFACT AND BOUNDARY TOGETHER

A strong case should explain what the designer did and provide a relevant artifact. It should also say what the artifact cannot establish. A Figma prototype can show an interaction model; it does not prove revenue, research quality or production adoption.

In my portfolio, Orkest supplies CRM hierarchy and shared-system discussion, piHub supplies multi-role financial workflow context, and Yarsha supplies a messaging-and-wallet design context. Those are distinct examples to inspect, not interchangeable labels on the same template.

USE A FOCUSED CONVERSATION
Use a focused conversation
Ask	Listen for
What was your part of this work?	A precise contribution and team boundary
Which decision was difficult?	Constraints, alternatives and an explicit trade-off
What happens when it fails?	States, retained context and recovery
How did the design reach implementation?	Contracts, review and actual limitations
What would you validate next?	A testable question instead of an invented outcome
CHECK COLLABORATION WITH A REAL PROBLEM

Bring a bounded example from your product and discuss the information needed to make a decision. This is a conversation about approach, not a request for unpaid production work. Notice whether the designer distinguishes facts from assumptions and asks about the current implementation before proposing a new screen.

For system work, ask how another designer or engineer would continue the pattern. For regulated or financial products, ask how design collaborates with the relevant domain and engineering owners rather than claiming authority over rules outside design.

CHOOSE THE ENGAGEMENT THAT FITS THE UNCERTAINTY

If you know the problem and need delivery, define the design slice and acceptance conditions. If you have conflicting symptoms, a bounded audit may be a better starting point. If you need an ongoing product partner, discuss how priorities, evidence and implementation review will be maintained.

I am based in Nepal and collaborate remotely. The relevant next step is to discuss your product, the contribution you need and what evidence would help both sides decide whether the fit is right.

text:
PRODUCT DESIGN / PRACTICAL NOTES

WHY A BEAUTIFUL INTERFACE CAN STILL HAVE POOR UX
WHY A BEAUTIFUL INTERFACE CAN STILL HAVE POOR UX

A polished screen can still leave the person unsure what to do, what changed or whether their work is safe. Review the decision the interface supports before judging the composition.

Nischhal Raj Subba
Originally published 2026-07-22
Updated 3 November 2026

ON THIS PAGE

Ask what the person can explain
Look for the state the presentation omits
Use four small diagnostic tasks
Distinguish motion from feedback
Repair the model before adding emphasis
ASK WHAT THE PERSON CAN EXPLAIN

A screenshot can look balanced while every action competes equally. Try a more specific review: what needs attention, what is the next action and what consequence will it have? If those answers are unclear, visual hierarchy is not yet supporting decision hierarchy.

This does not make visual craft unimportant. Typography, spacing and contrast are valuable because they help a person read relationships and priorities. The problem is treating their presence as evidence that the task works.

LOOK FOR THE STATE THE PRESENTATION OMITS

The default screen rarely shows what happens after a failed save, an unavailable permission or an empty result. Those states often carry the explanation a person most needs. Review them with the same care as the ideal composition.

The Yarsha contact-search frame is a useful example. It clearly reports No contact found, but the continuation still deserves inspection. Does the person know whether to change the query or use Invite? A clean layout can expose a good design question without proving it has been solved.

Yarsha contact search preserves the entered query, Contacts and Invite tabs, empty result and keyboard. Full original Figma frame; design content is sample data.
Open image ↗

Inspect the original Figma frame (access may be required)

USE FOUR SMALL DIAGNOSTIC TASKS
Explain the main action before selecting it.
Find the state and next action without relying on a color cue.
Trigger one error and recover without re-entering valid work.
Reach the same result using a keyboard and a narrow viewport.
DISTINGUISH MOTION FROM FEEDBACK

A movement or color change can signal activity without explaining the result. For a consequential action, feedback should establish whether the operation is still pending, completed, rejected or unresolved. Animation can support that explanation; it should not replace it.

Also review reduced-motion behavior. If the only way to understand a result is to follow an animated sequence, the product needs an equivalent explanation that remains usable without that sequence.

REPAIR THE MODEL BEFORE ADDING EMPHASIS

A larger primary button will not resolve an action whose meaning is unclear. First decide the task, state and consequence. Then use the visual system to make that decision easier to read.

For portfolio review, I prefer to connect a specific screen to the decision it supports and the questions still open. An attractive interface is evidence of craft. A task-based review supplies the additional evidence needed to judge the experience.
